## 6. Approach Formal Verification

To verify the proposed service-based approach to the lifecycle management of the FRMCS application instances, models of its status are developed. The models represent the view of the RCO and the view of the RCPM. Both models run in parallel and therefore their views on the state of an FRMCS application instance have to be synchronized.

[Figure 7](#fig_body_display_information-16-00712-f007) shows the simplified model of a state machine, representing the RCO’s view on the FRMCS application instance’s lifecycle state.

![Information 16 00712 g007](/information/information-16-00712/article_deploy/html/images/information-16-00712-g007-550.jpg "Information 16 00712 g007")

**Figure 7.**
State diagram of a simplified model representing the RCO’s view on the status of the FRMCS application instance.

In the following model description, the term “state” represents a specific condition or mode of operation, “event” is used for an occurrence that triggers a change in state, “transition” is a movement from one state to another, triggered by an event, and “action” is a specific operation performed when a transition occurs [[35](#B35-information-16-00712),[36](#B36-information-16-00712)].

In the NonInstantiated state (denoted by so1 for brevity), the application instance is not instantiated. When a request is received (instantiate event) from the railway cloud operator to instantiate an FRMCS application, the request is forwarded to the FRMCSAppInstLCM service (or just service) (instantiateReq action).

In the Instantiating state (abbreviated as so2), the application in the RCO is waiting for the result of the FRMCS application instantiation operation. The railway cloud operator may subscribe to notifications about the result of FRMCS application instantiation (subscribe event) and the managing application in the RCO (or just application) subscribes with the service to receive notifications about the result of the initiating operation (subscribeReq action). The railway cloud operator may cancel the initiation operation (cancel event) and the application requests from the service to cancel the instantiation (cancelReq action). The instantiation may be successful (instantiateRes(success) event) or may fail (instantiateRes(failed) event). The railway operator is notified about the result of the operation.

In the Failed.Instantiation state (abbreviated as so3), the FRMCS application instantiation is failed. The railway cloud operator may repeat the instantiation request (retry event) and the application requests from the service to retry the operation (retryReq action).

In the Instatiated.Stopped state (abbreviated as so4), the FRMCS application is instantiated but not started. The railway cloud operator may start the FRMCS application (start event) and the application sends a startReq request to the service. The railway cloud operator may terminate the FRMCS application instance (terminate event) and the application sends a terminateReq request to the service.

In the Starting state (abbreviated as so5), the FRMCS application instance is starting. The railway cloud operator may cancel the startup operation (cancel event), and thus, the application sends a request to the service to cancel the startup of the FRMCS application instance. The starting of the FRMCS application may be successful (startRes(success) event) or fail (startRes(failed) event).

In the Failed.Start state (abbreviated as so6), the startup of the FRMCS application has failed. The railway cloud operator may repeat the start request, and the application thus sends a request to the service to retry the operation or may cancel the starting operation.

In the Instatiated.Started state (abbreviated as so7), the FRMCS application has been instantiated and started. The railway cloud operator may stop the FRMCS application (stop event), and the application sends a stopReq request to the service. The railway cloud operator may terminate the FRMCS application instance, for which the application sends a terminateReq request to the service.

In the Stopping state (abbreviated as so8), the FRMCS application instance is stopping. The railway cloud operator may cancel the stop operation. The FRMCS application may be stopped (stopRes(success event) or the stopping of the FRMCS application may fail (stopRes(failed) event).

In the Failed.Stop state (abbreviated as so9), the FRMCS application stopping has failed. The railway cloud operator may repeat the stop request or cancel the stop operation.

In the Terminating (abbreviated as so10) state, the FRMCS application instance is terminating. The railway cloud operator may cancel the stop operation, the FRMCS application may be terminated, or the termination may fail.

In the Failed.Termination state (abbreviated as so11), the FRMCS application termination has failed. The railway cloud operator may repeat the termination request or cancel the operation.

[Figure 8](#fig_body_display_information-16-00712-f008) shows the simplified model of a state machine, representing the RCPM’s view on the FRMCS application instance’s lifecycle state. The state transitions in both models are triggered by HTTP methods, supported by the respective resources of the FRMCSAppInstLCM service.

![Information 16 00712 g008](/information/information-16-00712/article_deploy/html/images/information-16-00712-g008-550.jpg "Information 16 00712 g008")

**Figure 8.**
State diagram of a simplified model representing the RCPM’s view on the status of the FRMCS application instance.

In the Null state (abbreviated as sm1), the FRMCS application is not instantiated. In the RequestProcessing state (abbreviated as sm2), the requests from the application to instantiate an FRMCS application are authorized. In the ResourceAllocation&Configuration state (abbreviated as sm3), the instantiation request is authorized, the required resources are allocated, and the FRMCS application instance is configured. In the AppInst.Stopped state (abbreviated as sm4), the FRMCS application instance is created and configured, but not started. In the AppInst.Starting state (abbreviated as sm5), the FRMCS application instance is starting. In the AppInst.Started state (abbreviated as sm6), the FRMCS application instance is started. In the AppInst.Stopping state (abbreviated as sm7), the FRMCS application instance is stopping. In the AppInst.Terminating state (abbreviated as sm8), the FRMCS application instance is terminating.

To prove that both models are synchronized in time, they are formally described as LTSs. An LTS is a quadruple of a set of states, a set of events, a set of transitions, and an initial state. To provide a more concise description of the transitions and to make the following proposition and its proof more readable, short notations in brackets are used for the names of the events that are used.

**Definition** **1.**

Lrco = (Srco, Σ rco, →rco, srco0) denotes an LTS representing the FRMCS application instance’s lifecycle model, supported by the managing application in RCO, where

* Srco = { so1, so2, so3, so4, so5, so6, [so7, so8, so9, so10, so11} is the set of states;
* Σ rco = {instantiate [a1], subscribe [a2], subscribeRes [a3], notify(processing) [a4], cancel [a5], cancelRes [a6], retry [a7], retryRes [a8], instantiateRes(success) [a9], instantiateRes(failed) [a10], reject [a11], start [a12], startRes(failed) [a13], startRes(success) [a14], stop [a15], stopRes(failed) [a16], stopRes(success) [a17], terminated [a18], terminateRes(fail.started) [a19], terminateRes(fail.stopped) [a20], terminateRes(success) [a21], unsubscribe [a22], unsubscribeRes [a23], reject(stopped) [a24], reject(started) [a25], rejectRes [a26]} is the set of events;
* →rco = {(so1so2), (so2so2), (so2so2), (so2so2), (so2so3), (so3so3), (so3so2), (so2so2), (so2so4), (so2so1), (so2so1), (so1so1), (so4so5), (so5so5), (so5so5), (so5so6), (so6so6), (so6so5), (so5so4), (so5so4), (so5so7), (so7so8), (so8so8), (so8so8), (so8so9), (so9so9), (so9so8), (so8so7), (so8so7), (so8so4), (so4so10), (so7so10), (so10so10), (so10so10), (so10so11), (so11so11), (so11so10), (so10so10), (so10so4), (so10so7), (so10so1), (so1so1), (so1so1), (so10so4), (so10so7), (so4so4), (so7so7) } is the set of transitions;
* srco0 = [so1] is the initial state.

**Definition** **2.**

Lrcpm = (Srcpm, Σ rcpm, →rcpm, srcpm0) denotes an LTS representing the FRMCS application instance’s lifecycle model, supported by the cloud management service in RCPM, where

* Srcpm = { sm1, sm2, sm3, sm4, sm5, sm6, sm7, sm8} is the set of states;
* Σ rcpm = {instantiateReq [t1], unauthorizedRequest [t2], authorizedRequest [t3], subscriptionReq [t4], cancelReq [t5], cancelApp.Res [t6], retryReq [t7], rejectReq [t8], rejectAppRes [t9], instantiateAppRes(failed) [t10], unsubscribeReq [t11], instantiateAppRes(success) [t12], startReq [t13], startAppRes(failed) [t14], startAppRes(success) [t15], stopReq [t16], stopAppRes [t17], stopAppRes(success) [t18], terminateReq [t19], terminateAppRes(success) [t20], rejectAppRes(started) [t21], terminateAppRes(fail,started) [t22], rejectAppRes(stopped) [t23], terminateAppRes(fail,stopped) [t24]} is the set of events;
* →rcpm = { (sm1sm2), (sm2sm1), (sm2sm3), (sm3sm3), (sm3sm3), (sm3sm3), (sm3sm3), (sm3sm3), (sm3sm1), (sm3sm1), (sm1sm1), (sm3sm4), (sm3sm5), (sm5sm5), (sm5sm5), (sm5sm5), (sm5sm5), (sm5sm4), (sm5sm4), (sm5sm6), (sm6sm7), (sm7sm7), (sm7sm7), (sm7sm7), (sm7sm7), (sm7sm6), (sm7sm6), (sm7sm4), (sm4sm8), (sm6sm8), (sm8sm8), (sm8sm8), (sm8sm8), (sm8sm8), (sm8sm6), (sm8sm6), (sm8sm4), (sm8sm4), (sm8sm1)} is the set of transitions;
* srcpm0 = [sm1] is the initial state.
* To prove that the models representing the FRMCS application instance’s status are synchronized in time, the concept of synchronization in the states of two LTSs is used. The formal mathematical definition of this concept may be found in [[33](#B33-information-16-00712)]. The idea is to identify such tuples of states where (1) one state in a tuple belongs to one LTS and the other state belongs to the other LTS, and (2) a bijection function exists between the transitions starting in a state in a tuple and terminating in a state in a tuple.

**Proposition** **1.**

Let R represent a set of tuples of states in Lrco and Lrcpm (i.e., R ⊆ Srco × Srcpm), where R = {(so1, sm1), (so4, sm4), (so7, sm6)}. R is the synchronization between the states in Lrco and Lrcpm.

**Proof** **1.**

We identify a bijection function of transition between the states in tuples of R, which is shown in [Table 3](#table_body_display_information-16-00712-t003). In [Table 3](#table_body_display_information-16-00712-t003), the first column describes the abstract meaning of the transition, and the second column indicates the tuple of initial states for the transition and the tuple of terminating states for the transition. The third and fourth columns show the transitions in Lrco and Lrcpm, respectively.

**Table 3.**
Bijective function of transition sequences in models representing the FRMCS application instance’s status.

![](https://pub.mdpi-res.com/img/table.png)

Therefore, R is synchronized between states. □

This means that Lrco and Lrcpm have synchronized-in-time views on the FRMCS application instance’s status.

## 7. API Emulation

Latency is a key performance indicator for critical FRMCS applications. An experiment was conducted to assess the latency injected by the proposed APIs. The experiment was conducted in a laboratory environment due to the lack of real cloud infrastructure for rail transport.

The communication between FRMCS management applications in the RCO and the designed services in the RCPM is simulated. As the RESTful APIs are HTTP-based, the experimental setup includes components demonstrating the functionality of both the server and the client. The RESTful load consists of POST requests with the domain-specific data in JSON format generated by a Java-based HTTP multi-threaded client. The server component consists of two docker instances: one instance enables the REST endpoint and the Cassandra client, and the other enables the Cassandra server, providing a lightweight virtualized storage service. args.summary:
This academic paper, published in *Information* (2025, Volume 16, Issue 8, Article 712), authored by Ivaylo Atanasov, Evelina Pencheva, and Kamelia Nikolova, presents a service-based approach to managing virtualized applications for the Future Railway Mobile Communication System (FRMCS). FRMCS is a global standard designed as the successor to GSM-R, based on 5G mobile communications, offering ultra-fast, secure, wireless voice, video, and data transmission with high reliability and low latency.

The paper proposes an architectural framework for Railway Management Automation and Orchestration (RMAO) following ETSI NFV principles, with the Railway Cloud Platform (RCP) and Railway Cloud Platform Manager (RCPM) managing virtualized FRMCS applications. Key contributions include:

- Identification of requirements for FRMCS application package and lifecycle management (onboarding, instantiation, scaling, termination, etc.) based on use case analysis.
- Design of RESTful APIs (FRMCSAppPackageMgnt and FRMCSAppInstLCM services) for managing application packages and instance lifecycles.
- Formal verification of the APIs using Labeled Transition Systems (LTS) to prove synchronization between the RCO's (Railway Cloud Operator) and RCPM's views of application instance states.
- Evaluation of API-induced latency through emulation, which is a key performance indicator for critical FRMCS applications.

The FRMCS specification is expected to be completed by the end of 2026. The paper emphasizes that virtualization enables flexible deployment, task segregation for safety, and cost-effective software migration for railway systems that must provide 99.999% reliability. The proposed RESTful APIs are lightweight, scalable, and technology-independent. The formal verification mathematically proves that the state models of the managing and managed entities are synchronized in time.

One of its main goals is to bring reactions in order to recover operational or organizational functionalities for successfully accomplishing their objectives [1]. More speciﬁcally, cyber-resilience provides continuity of service regardless of the adversity con-ditions it encounters (e.g., failure, cyber-attack, environmental dangers, etc.) [2], since it begins with the assumption that adversities cannot be avoided, and that their outcomes can either be a breakdown or a successful attack.
Cyber-resilience faces two types of adversities, the intentional ones which are cybersecurity-related and the unintentional ones which are safety-related. Since cyber-resilience consid-ers both of these types of adversities, it is important to integrate safety and cybersecurity in order to support and enhance cyber-resilience. But also, cyber-resilience can balance their functions and operations, to support their harmonic integration. In a more global approach, the integrated safety and cybersecurity make a system more resilient in the face of adversities, thus it is understood that both safety and cybersecurity are the essence of cyber-resilience [3].
In the literature, there are standards, guidelines, and approaches for applying cyber-resilience practices to systems and organizations, such as Robustness, Redundancy, Re-sourcefulness, and Rapidity framework (R4), NIST [2], CERT [4], ISO 22301 [5], ISO 22316 [6], Smart Mature Resilience (SMR) [7], and DHS-CRR [8]. R4 is a cyber-resilience oriented framework which inspires metric construction for quantitatively assessments [9] and uses graph invariants for future wireless and optical networks of 5G systems [10].
The standards NIST, CERT, ISO 22301, and ISO 22316 can assist the organization to decide what kind of work line can be implemented in order to guarantee organizational and operational continuity. SMR frameworks can provide city cyber-resilience. DHS-CRR frameworks can ensure continuity for all types of critical infrastructure.
It is obvious that there is a variety of standards, guidelines, and approaches in order to 7 Chapter 1 – Introduction guarantee cyber-resilience, which have also the advantage of improving the cyber surviv-ability and vice versa [11]. However, up to our knowledge the aforementioned standards, guidelines, and approaches are limited in terms of techniques, do not include the sup-port of the safety and cybersecurity integration, and are mostly linked to cybersecurity and less to safety [2]. However, safety is the most signiﬁcant property to be considered in safety-critical systems. This is because the main focus for these systems is to prevent harm on humans and environment.
Moreover, as technology advances, one promising way for enhancing safety and cy-bersecurity integration lies in the evolution of railway systems with the integration of 5G technology. This intergation holds the potential to revolutionize railway operations, enabling real-time data transmission, enhanced communication between trains and infras-tructure, and boosting both of safety and eﬃciency in railway operations.
1.1 Safety orchestrator for anomaly treatment and mitigation In general, safety is an important property for Network Function Virtualization (NFV), because NFV applications can be deployed and implemented in critical systems. NFV is a principle of separating network functions from the hardware they run on by using virtual hardware abstraction [12]. In case NFV is used in industry such as railway, it is understood that safety is an important property for this sector. This is because the main asset for protection is the human life. For example, an essential component of a train breaks down, while the train is moving. This can have an impact on the people that it carries, the people in the surrounding, and the surrounding environment itself.
More speciﬁcally, safety is able to interact with other properties as well. According to the ENISA standard [13] safety is a subset of the reliability, maintainability, availability, and integrity properties. In this way it is understood that safety has the ability to interact with these aforementioned properties while considering their impact to humans and en-vironment. For the railway though, according to Reliability, Availability, Maintainability, and Safety (RAMS) standard [14], safety is a subset of the reliability, maintainability, and availability properties. This speciﬁc standard uses all its properties for a systematic management process in railway. However, integrity is also considered in safety, with the Safety Integrity Level (SIL). This is because, integrity is one of the Key Performance Indicators (KPI) of safety. More speciﬁcally, safety has the ability to interact with the 8 1.1. Safety orchestrator for anomaly treatment and mitigation availability, maintainability, integrity, and reliability properties, while considering in each one of them, the impact to humans and environment.
Nowadays though, railway systems face cyber-attacks more and more, and especially with the exponential use of virtualization technologies, such as Network function Virtual-ization (NFV) [15]. This is because, virtualization technologies provide many advantages and improvements. These improvements are ﬂexibility, scalability, ubiquity, programma-bility, and dynamicity. Even though they bring many improvements, they introduce many vulnerabilities as well. Hence, in railway sector not only safety is considered, but also cy-bersecurity. For example, NFV handles services for an autonomous vehicle. In case a cyber-attack happens in one of the NFV services, it can make the vehicle uncontrollable.
This can lead to an impact on humans and environment. However, such an integration of safety and cybersecurity in a methodology for railway sector, is not yet succeeded even though it is a stressed point in both academia [16] and industry [17].
In railway sector, safety and cybersecurity interact with each other, and thus they are interdependent. More speciﬁcally the functionalities of safety can violate the functionali-ties of cybersecurity and vice versa. As an example, cybersecurity may ask for “no brake force" in a train, as a way to mitigate a cybersecurity anomaly and safety blocks this speciﬁc action, because it goes against its safety measures. Likewise, safety may block the update of the system that is responsible for locking the doors of the train while it is mov-ing. In this case, the system is vulnerable to cyber attacks. However, not only the conﬂict between safety and cybersecurity should be addressed, but there are also challenges for ensuring safety.
Summing up, there are challenges to be addressed for ensuring safety. These challenges are: (i) the detection and mitigation of a variety of safety anomalies in a more compre-hensive way, and (ii) the management of safety and cybersecurity interdependency. More speciﬁcally, there are many solutions in the literature for addressing a variety of safety-related anomalies in NFV and by extension in railway. Up to our knowledge, none of these solutions provide one single methodology that comprises all of the aforementioned properties as a whole. This is important because it allows us to understand all anomalies that aﬀect safety even if they come from other properties. In addition, there are solu-tions in the literature that provide a safety and cybersecurity integration. However, in these solutions safety and cybersecurity are considered independently. To the best of our knowledge, there are no solutions that provide a methodology that considers safety and cybersecurity as interdependent. Furthermore, there are no solutions for an NFV safety 9 Chapter 1 – Introduction architecture that use availability and integrity as common properties between safety and cybersecurity.
To address these needs, our thesis presents two chapters of contribution: the ﬁrst focuses on developing a safety ontology that integrates safety and cybersecurity con-siderations, while the second introduces a safety orchestrator designed to manage the interdependency between safety and cybersecurity eﬀectively. These contributions aim to enhance the overall safety and security of NFV and railway systems.
1.1.1 Safety ontology Ontology is a good option for addressing the aforementioned challenges since it is an explicit speciﬁcation of a conceptualization where the knowledge of a domain is repre-sented in a declarative formalism [18]. This makes it possible to represent the diﬀerent types of anomalies in relation to safety. According to this uniformized representation the reasoner (piece of software) is able to infer logical consequences. These consequences make it possible to understand whether a safety-related anomaly is also a cybersecurity-related one.
In the railway environment, the necessity of utilizing a safety ontology arises from the complex and heterogeneous nature of systems and components, particularly the coex-istence of Information Technology (IT) and Operational Technology (OT) technologies.
Railway systems often comprise a multitude of interconnected elements, including legacy and modern equipment, each with its own set of functionalities, interfaces, and communi-cation protocols. These systems may vary signiﬁcantly in terms of their maturity and age, with some components being decades-old embedded systems that lack modern cybersecu-rity features. Moreover, the integration of IT and OT technologies introduces additional layers of complexity, as these systems traditionally operate in separate domains with dis-tinct safety and security considerations. In such a diverse and interconnected environment, understanding the interdependency between safety and cybersecurity becomes paramount for ensuring the overall cyber-resilience of railway operations. By employing a safety ontol-ogy, which provides a structured representation of safety-related concepts, relationships, and dependencies within the railway ecosystem, stakeholders can systematically analyze and assess the impact of cybersecurity threats on safety-critical functions. This enables proactive risk management strategies and facilitates informed decision-making processes to safeguard both passengers and critical railway infrastructure from potential hazards and vulnerabilities.
10 1.1. Safety orchestrator for anomaly treatment and mitigation In order to diﬀerentiate the safety anomalies from the cybersecurity ones. An ontology-based solution is a good way to automate this process. Thus, it is possible to ﬁnd ontology-based solutions for each one of the safety-related properties independently. However, in the literature there are no ontology-based solutions for safety considering all the proper-ties related to it as a whole. Moreover, there are no ontology-based solutions that provide a safety and cybersecurity interdependency. This has the eﬀect of limiting the decision-making process that is used for distinguishing the anomalies created in a system. Fur-thermore, this prevents from taking into consideration the interdependency of safety and cybersecurity.
To this end our solution proposes: (i) a new ontology for ensuring safety in NFV framework, and (ii) speciﬁc rules to be used by the reasoner. Our proposed ontology is used by an orchestrator that handles safety in a NFV framework. This ontology includes: (i) the description of safety and the properties related to it (i.e., reliability, availability, maintainability, and integrity) as classes, (ii) the concerned elements for each property as sub-classes, and (iii) the breakdown types for the potential adversities as object properties.
Our proposed rules allow us to automate the decision-making process. This is because the reasoner needs the rules to make a decision. According to this decision a NFV safety orchestrator is able to modify the plan of mitigation. With this modiﬁcation it is possible to avoid potential safety and cybersecurity conﬂicts.
1.1.2 Safety orchestrator Our NFV safety orchestrator for railway solution handles the virtualized services and functions of a rolling stock. This orchestrator is called STELAC and is able to focus on the phase of the safety and cybersecurity interactions during anomaly mitigation. This orchestrator is the core of our safety architecture for NFV frameworks. In this architec-ture, each safety-related property corresponds to a speciﬁc orchestrator for handling the appropriate anomalies. Each one of the safety-related orchestrators uses agents to be able to detect potential anomalies from each one of the modules of the NFV framework [19].
These orchestrators do not treat the anomaly, but they send it to our safety orchestra-tor. The safety orchestrator is then able to: (i) identify the anomaly and its type, (ii) understand if this anomaly is also cybersecurity-related, (iii) decide the mitigation plan while considering the safety and cybersecurity interdependency, (iv) issue the mitigation plan to the NFV. The advantages of our proposal are: (i) it allows us to have a whole image of safety-related anomalies, and (ii) it provides the ability to handle the safety and 11 Chapter 1 – Introduction cybersecurity interdependency.
1.2 Conclusion In conclusion, our thesis explores the critical concept of cyber-resilience and its im-plications, particularly in the context of safety-critical systems, with a focus on Network Function Virtualization (NFV) in the railway sector. The discussion underscores the intri-cate interplay between safety and cybersecurity, emphasizing their interdependency and the challenges that arise when ensuring both in the face of evolving technologies and cyber threats.
The thesis delves into existing standards, guidelines, and approaches for implementing cyber-resilience, highlighting their strengths and limitations. It identiﬁes a gap in current solutions, particularly in the integration of safety and cybersecurity and the lack of a uniﬁed methodology addressing their interdependence.
To address these challenges, our thesis introduces the concept of a Safety Orches-trator, speciﬁcally designed for anomaly treatment and mitigation in NFV applications.
The proposed Safety Orchestrator, named STELAC, incorporates a Safety Ontology to distinguish safety-related anomalies from cybersecurity ones.
In essence, our thesis contributes to the ongoing discourse on cyber-resilience by proposing innovative methodologies to enhance safety in the realm of NFV, addressing the complexities arising from the integration of safety and cybersecurity. As technologies evolve and threats persist, such holistic approaches become imperative for ensuring the robustness and adaptability of critical systems in the face of adversities.
Additionally, our thesis is structured into several chapters to provide a comprehensive understanding of the subject matter. Chapter 2: The State of the Art, explores the current landscape of cyber-resilience in safety-critical systems, analyzing existing standards and approaches. Chapter 3: The Safety Ontology, introduces a novel approach to organizing safety-related concepts and dependencies. Chapter 4: The Safety Orchestrator, presents our proposed solution for anomaly treatment and mitigation in NFV applications. Finally, the conclusion chapter summarizes the key ﬁndings and contributions of our research, highlighting the importance of holistic approaches in ensuring the resilience of critical systems.

2.2 Safety ontology Ontologies play a pivotal role in system modeling due to their capacity to comprehen-sively describe entire systems along with their intricate components and subsystems. The essence of an ontology lies in its expression as the study of what exists within a speciﬁc context, as articulated by Gruber [18].
The power of ontologies stems from their ability to go beyond mere representation and delve into the semantics and relationships that deﬁne the elements within a system.
By encapsulating knowledge about entities, their attributes, and the associations between them, ontologies provide a structured and formalized framework for understanding the contextual existence of various components within a given domain.
In the realm of system modeling, ontologies serve as a foundational tool for capturing not just the physical entities but also the conceptual and semantic relationships that gov-16 2.2. As organizations grapple with the interconnected challenges of safety and cybersecu-rity, leveraging ontologies in system modeling becomes instrumental. 2.2.1 Ontologies for cyber-resilience Resilience in IT systems and cybersecurity has emerged as a critical area of research and development, particularly in response to the growing threat landscape posed by cyber incidents. Several innovative frameworks, ontologies, and methodologies have been pro-posed to enhance the resilience of IT systems and eﬀectively respond to cyber threats. A breakdown of key contributions is as follows.
One approach involves the development of a framework based on ontologies and logical inference [41]. This framework is designed to meet the requirements of resilient IT systems, particularly in terms of response to and recovery from cyber incidents. By leveraging ontologies, it aims to provide a structured representation of knowledge and facilitate logical inference to enhance system resilience.
Several studies focus on the development of ontologies speciﬁcally tailored for cyber resilience [42], [43]. These ontologies aim to formalize the concept of cyber resilience, addressing both individual citizens and broader domains such as cybersecurity in the electric power sector. By deﬁning constitutive concepts and integrating domain-speciﬁc knowledge, these ontologies serve as valuable resources for enhancing resilience through eﬀective decision-making and knowledge management.
Given the critical importance of cybersecurity in sectors like electric power, speciﬁc attention has been directed towards developing resilience strategies [33]. Process models and design propositions have been formulated to address the unique challenges faced by the electric power sector. Through empirical validation and digital twin implementations, these models provide insights for both further research and practical applications aimed at ensuring resilience in critical infrastructure.
17 Chapter 2 – State of the art Another notable contribution involves the use of ontologies, particularly those based on Cyber Threat Intelligence (CTI), for risk monitoring [44]. By extending existing on-tologies and aligning them with standardized concepts such as STIX (Structured Threat Information eXpression), these frameworks enhance the capability of Security Information Event Management (SIEM) systems to monitor and respond to cyber threats eﬀectively.
Additionally, eﬀorts have been made to develop ontology schemes speciﬁcally focused on resilient computer systems [45]. These schemes outline the operational cycle of resilient computer systems, delineating key stages such as preparation, threat detection, response, and recovery. By providing a taxonomy and ontology of resilient computer systems, these frameworks contribute to the understanding and implementation of resilience strategies in the face of cyber threats.
In summary, the state-of-the-art in resilient IT systems and cybersecurity encompasses a diverse range of approaches, including ontologies, frameworks, and process models. These contributions aim to enhance the ability of IT systems and critical infrastructure to with-stand and recover from cyber incidents, ultimately bolstering resilience in the face of evolving threats.
Furthermore, a common thread across these papers is the recognition of the close relationship between cyber-resilience and cybersecurity. While the focus is primarily on mitigating cyber threats and ensuring the continuity of operations in the face of disrup-tions, it is important to note that cyber-resilience does not solely encompass cybersecurity concerns. Rather, it encompasses a broader spectrum of considerations, including safety.
Although safety is equally vital for ensuring the overall resilience of systems, the research highlighted here primarily emphasizes cybersecurity measures and strategies. This un-derscores the interconnected nature of cybersecurity and cyber-resilience, emphasizing the need for comprehensive approaches that address both aspects to eﬀectively safeguard critical infrastructure and IT systems against evolving threats and disruptions. For this reason, it is essential to also examine safety ontologies to determine whether existing frameworks can contribute to enhancing cyber-resilience.

Safety ontology Safety ontologies In the realm of safety management, ontologies are increasingly recognized for their versatility and eﬀectiveness in acquiring and structuring safety risk knowledge. By orga-nizing this knowledge into a uniﬁed framework comprising distinct classes such as project, construction activity, risk factor, and risk consequence, ontologies provide a comprehen-sive understanding of safety hazards and their associated management strategies [46]. This structured approach not only facilitates the identiﬁcation and assessment of potential risks but also enables proactive measures to mitigate them eﬀectively. Moreover, the incorpo-ration of case-based reasoning mechanisms within safety ontologies oﬀers a sophisticated decision-making approach for addressing dynamic safety challenges [47].
Beyond risk management, ontologies play a pivotal role in leveraging existing databases to extract and represent safety-related information. Through semantic structuring, ontolo-gies enhance the interpretability and usability of vast datasets, enabling stakeholders to uncover hidden insights and identify emerging safety trends [48]. This capability is par-ticularly valuable in industries where data-driven decision-making is paramount, such as construction, manufacturing, and transportation.
However, the true potential of ontologies lies in their integration with complementary technologies and methodologies. By combining ontologies with advanced computer vision algorithms, for example, organizations can develop sophisticated knowledge graphs capa-ble of autonomously detecting and analyzing safety hazards in real-time [49]. This integra-tion not only streamlines hazard identiﬁcation processes but also enhances the accuracy and reliability of safety assessments, thereby minimizing the risk of workplace accidents and injuries. Similarly, the fusion of ontologies with wireless network technologies oﬀers new avenues for proactive hazard detection and prevention. By leveraging real-time data from wireless sensors and devices, organizations can identify potential safety threats and implement timely interventions to mitigate risks [50].
Expanding beyond traditional safety domains, ontologies are increasingly applied in broader contexts, including environmental sustainability and product development pro-cesses. In the pursuit of sustainability, companies are embracing ontological models along-side green processes and Design for X (DFX) methodologies to address environmental concerns throughout the product lifecycle [51]. This holistic approach not only promotes eco-friendly practices but also enhances organizational resilience and competitiveness in an increasingly environmentally conscious market. Similarly, in industries such as con-struction, where safety management is paramount, the integration of computer vision 19 Chapter 2 – State of the art and ontology techniques oﬀers a novel approach to hazard identiﬁcation and mitigation [52]. By aligning with safety regulations and leveraging prior knowledge, this integrated framework facilitates proactive safety management practices, ultimately enhancing on-site safety outcomes and reducing the incidence of workplace accidents.
In conclusion, ontologies represent a powerful tool for enhancing safety management practices across diverse industries and domains. Whether in the context of risk manage-ment, data-driven decision-making, or sustainability initiatives, ontologies oﬀer a versatile framework for organizing, interpreting, and leveraging safety-related information. By em-bracing the integration of ontologies with emerging technologies and methodologies, orga-nizations can unlock new possibilities for improving safety outcomes, fostering innovation, and driving sustainable growth.
It is important to acknowledge that while ontologies oﬀer signiﬁcant capabilities in en-hancing safety management practices, the scope of this discussion does not encompass all safety-related properties as outlined by ENISA. While ontologies undoubtedly contribute to aspects of safety management, particularly in risk assessment and hazard identiﬁca-tion, they represent just one component of a broader safety and cybersecurity strategy.
Organizations must adopt a holistic approach to safety management that addresses all relevant properties and considerations outlined by authoritative bodies like ENISA to en-sure comprehensive protection against evolving safety and security threats. Thus, while ontologies provide valuable insights and organizational structures, they are part of a larger ecosystem of safety management tools and practices aimed at safeguarding critical assets and infrastructure from potential risks and vulnerabilities.
For this reason, it becomes imperative to delve deeper into the realm of safety-related properties within ontologies, exploring their incorporation and representation within these structured frameworks.
Reliability ontologies Reliability with respect to ontologies is expressed as a way to make ontologies reliable, or to use ontologies for increasing reliability in various systems. Agile methodology uses agile principles and practices for ontology development. In this way it is possible to uti-lize software engineering to build reliable ontologies [53]. Moreover, ontology alignment is a way to create reliable ontologies. In [54] machine learning techniques are used to automatically align ontologies to make them more reliable.
However, ontologies are able to be used in various methodologies in order to provide a 20 2.2. Safety ontology variety of diﬀerent types of reliability. In general an ontology-based text mining method-ology is able to maximize system reliability, since it is able to extract knowledge from databases [55]. There are many technologies and methods in order to use semantic web and ontologies for providing reliable services. This is because the use of semantic technolo-gies in the modeling of a multi-agent system, are very eﬀective in increasing coordination and interoperability, as seen in [56]. Furthermore, ontologies are able to assist into making the numerical simulation techniques more reliable. This can happen with ontology-based text and data mining techniques, as seen in [57].
Availability ontologies Ontologies for ensuring availability are not widely researched in the literature, up to our knowledge. However, in [58], ontologies are used to provide and ensure heteroge-neous knowledge for a speciﬁc concept. By combining these ontologies with optimization algorithms, it is possible to provide high data availability.
To sum up, availability is closely linked to reliability and maintainability. Once a system is reliable and maintainable, then it is possible to satisfy availability [59].
Maintainability ontologies Maintainability is an attribute that is included in dependability. In order to be able to understand all attributes of dependability but also to compare them, it is possible to use a dependability rating ontology [60]. Thus, it is possible to obtain knowledge about the attribute of maintainability but also in relation to the other attributes. Moreover, ontologies can be created by extracting them from other ontologies or by creating them from scratch. The approach to develop an ontology is able to aﬀect the maintainability.
Thus, the evaluation of the ontology development is very important. In [61], the authors propose a methodology for evaluating ontology development from scratch.
Furthermore, it is important to be able to create maintainable ontologies. For achiev-ing this a methodology is proposed in [62] which is able to construct ontologies using a template-based approach for ontology modelling and instantiation. However, ontologies can be also used to enhance maintainability in a system. In [63] an ontology model is pro-posed to facilitate maintenance strategies selection and assessment. And in [64] ontologies are used for data accessing in order to enhance system maintainability.

This is a doctoral thesis (PhD dissertation) by Dionysia Varvarigou, submitted at Université de Bretagne Occidentale - Brest in 2024, titled "Integration of cybersecurity and safety to improve the resilience of industrial railway control systems." The thesis focuses on cyber-resilience in safety-critical systems, particularly in railway control systems using Network Function Virtualization (NFV).

**Key Problem:** Cyber-resilience must address both intentional (cybersecurity) and unintentional (safety) adversities. Current frameworks prioritize cybersecurity over safety, lacking integrated approaches. Railway systems face increasing cyber-attacks as virtualization technologies (NFV) are adopted, creating safety-cybersecurity interdependencies where safety measures can conflict with cybersecurity measures and vice versa.

**Main Contributions:**

1. **Safety Ontology (Chapter 3):** A novel ontology that integrates safety and cybersecurity considerations for NFV frameworks. It includes classes for safety-related properties (reliability, availability, maintainability, integrity), their sub-classes, and breakdown types for potential adversities. Rules are defined to automate decision-making and help the reasoner distinguish safety anomalies from cybersecurity ones, enabling proactive risk management.

2. **Safety Orchestrator - STELAC (Chapter 4):** A safety orchestrator for NFV frameworks in railway rolling stock that manages the interdependency between safety and cybersecurity during anomaly mitigation. STELAC can: (i) identify anomalies and their types, (ii) determine if an anomaly is also cybersecurity-related, (iii) decide mitigation plans while considering safety-cybersecurity interdependency, and (iv) issue mitigation plans to NFV. It includes a conflict management module for handling safety-cybersecurity interdependencies and a certification indicator for mechanisms.

**Key Concepts:** The thesis argues that safety and cybersecurity are interdependent and must be integrated for effective cyber-resilience. Safety is defined as a subset of reliability, maintainability, availability, and integrity (per ENISA), with RAMS standard used for railway. The NFV safety architecture assigns each safety-related property to a specific orchestrator that detects anomalies, while STELAC serves as the centralized decision-maker.

**Evaluation:** The proposed solutions were evaluated through case studies including a 5G use case and a railway use case, with testing on stability, fault injection, and scalability.

This summary will be used by a downstream research agent, so it's crucial to maintain the key details without losing essential information.

Here is the raw content of the webpage:

<webpage_content>
On Temporal Isolation Assessment in Virtualized Railway Signaling as a Service Systems Domenico Cotroneo, Luigi De Simone, Roberto Natella Universit` a degli Studi di Napoli Federico II, Naples, Italy {cotroneo, luigi.desimone, roberto.natella}@unina.it Abstract—Railway signaling systems provide numerous critical functions at different safety level, to correctly implement the entire transport ecosystem. Today, we are witnessing the increasing use of the cloud and virtualization technologies in such mixed-criticality systems, with the main goal of reducing costs, improving reliability, while providing orchestration capabilities.
Unfortunately, virtualization includes several issues for assessing temporal isolation, which is critical for safety-related standards like EN50128. In this short paper, we envision leveraging the real-time ﬂavor of a general-purpose hypervisor, like Xen, to build the Railway Signaling as a Service (RSaaS) systems of the future. We provide a preliminary background, highlighting the need for a systematic evaluation of the temporal isolation to demonstrate the feasibility of using general-purpose hypervisors in the safety-critical context for certiﬁcation purposes.
Index Terms—Railway signaling, Virtualization, Temporal isolation, Xen, Cloud computing I. INTRODUCTION Railway signaling includes complex systems that aim to guarantee the safety of rail infrastructure, the environment, and human beings. It connects several sensors and other subsystems via signals, which allow synchronization and transmission of control data to different vital and non-vital components within the rail infrastructure [1]. Generally, this infrastructure includes several modules on-board trains, whose task is to manage the safety of the train itself, keep the appropriate speed of the vehicle, and prevent collisions.
Usually, rail interlocking plants are kept strictly close to tracks to be controlled and rely on complex architectures and several costly cabling and communication systems. These architectures forced railway providers to rent or buy buildings in speciﬁc locations to house them.
Today, we are witnessing the use of cloud and virtualization technologies to develop a way of housing everything remotely, by implementing a Railway Signaling as a Service (RSaaS) system. This new model will reduce dramatically operational and capital costs that companies must support; moreover, it results in innovations since rail signals can be easily controlled by exploiting smart sensors, which enable new ways of fault diagnosis, failure predictions, and predictive maintenance, increasing the overall transportation effectiveness [2], [3].
Besides railway, virtualization is increasingly used also in other industrial domains, such as avionic, automotive, Industrial Internet of Things (IIoT), and telco systems with the recent development of 5G [4]–[10]. Commonly, industrial practitioners develop mixed-criticality systems, which integrate functionalities at different safety and/or time-critical levels into common platforms to reduce the size, weight, power, and cost of hardware. This leads to numerous challenges, especially when adopting virtualization technologies, since safety, fault-tolerance, and real-timeliness must be guaranteed at the same time at different levels. Indeed, mixed-criticality systems have to satisfy stringent requirements imposed by safety-critical standards (e.g., [11], [12], [13]), which mostly refer to temporal and spatial isolation among software component.
Spatial isolation includes the capability of isolating code and data between domains (e.g., virtual machines (VMs)), preventing tasks to alter private data belonging to other tasks. Instead, temporal isolation is about limiting the impact of resource consumption (e.g., tasks running on a VM) on the performance of other software components (e.g., tasks running on the other VMs). Compared to spatial isolation, which is often guaranteed by only using hardware-assisted mechanisms (e.g., MMU), temporal isolation remains a critical and open research problem [14]–[18]. To exacerbate the problem, the above-mentioned standards also recommend providing documentation about evidence of a fail-safe and/or fail-stop behavior for such systems, which ultimately prevent failures leading to human and cost losses.
In this short paper, we depict our ongoing work of devel-oping an RSaaS. We describe a Proof of Concept (PoC) ac-cording to the classical fault-tolerant 2oo2 schema, along with a methodology for evaluating temporal isolation. The PoC is currently implemented on top of a real-time ﬂavor of the Xen hypervisor and PREEMPT RT-patched guests, which are be-coming increasingly a choice as a basis for safety-critical virtu-alized systems since it provides several features for supporting real-time applications along cloud computing support [19].
Further, we highlight the need for a systematic assessment of temporal isolation by leveraging well-known Design of Experiments (DoE) [20] to rigorously estimate the impact and signiﬁcance of the numerous existing factors in this kind of en-vironment, against various operational scenarios. The objective is to provide guidelines to properly ﬁne-tune these systems to provide temporal isolation evidence for certiﬁcation purposes.
The rest of the paper is organized as follows. Section II introduces the proposal. Section III shows preliminary results.
Section IV analyzes representative real-time hypervisors in the state of the art. Section V concludes the paper.
arXiv:2208.14109v1 [cs.DC] 30 Aug 2022 II. PROPOSAL In this section, we provide the background needed for under-standing the proposed RSaaS PoC. We highlight the peculiar-ities of the host side, guest side. We brieﬂy introduce the need for temporal isolation assessment for certiﬁcation purposes.
A. Railway Signaling as a Service (RSaaS) PoC In this work, we study the feasibility of developing a system that provides RSaaS by leveraging virtualization and cloud technologies. Figure 1 envisions the high-level architecture, in which both the rail control center and station equipment are deployed in cloud data centers, replacing physical boards with several virtualized domains (e.g., virtual machines) running on top of high-performance real-time hypervisors. The data communication system (DCS) provides the communication between trains and ground carrying Communications Based Train Control (CBTC) signaling information and other telecommunication services onboard, like CCTV. The DCS network guarantees bidirectional, reliable, and secured exchange of data between equipment of the train control subsystems (e.g. zone controllers, interlocking, and carborne controllers). Wayside equipment is omitted for the sake of simplicity.
Fig. 1.
High-level architecture of a Communications Based Train Control (CBTC).
In general, signaling includes fail-safe applications, which require fail-stop approaches, with temporal monitoring of critical voting or time monitoring tasks. Indeed, CBTC signaling systems include several replicas for each component, which send the result of their measurements to a component, namely, the voter, which compares the results and eventually takes a decision by notifying if an error occurred or by acknowledging that the service is properly working. The most common conﬁguration to guarantee fault-tolerance is the 2oo2 schema, in which there are 2 replicas for each system, the voter compares received values, and if they are different, an error is notiﬁed. When an error is notiﬁed, the train can be stopped and brought back to a fail-safe state. In order to properly handle common-mode errors, the 2oo2 Hot Redundancy (2oo2HR) schema is introduced. This schema considers two independent and isolated sections, i.e., a master section that is running by default, and a stand-by section that will be activated if an error occurs in the master section.
According to the classical fault tolerance mechanism used in the railway domain, Figure 2 shows the currently implemented PoC, which emulates a 2oo2 system, with 3 unprivileged virtual machines, two of them simulating the two replicas of a sensor, while one acting as a voter. The two replicas generate several values (simulating a measurement) over time, and they will send them to the voter. There is a probability that the two measurements will be different. When the voter receives a measurement from one of the two replicas will send an ACK to the sender. When both measurements will be received, the voter will compare them, returning a string that will indicate if the message received contain the same value.
Fig. 2. High-level PoC 2oo2 architecture.
The VMs are managed by a privileged VM (pVM), running side by side with unprivileged VMs on top of a real-time hypervisor. In this short paper, we leverage the real-time ﬂavor of the well-known Xen hypervisor for the pVM, and PREEMPT RT-patched Linux as a guest OS for unprivileged VMs.
1) RT-Xen vs RTDS Xen: The Xen hypervisor is an open-source type-1 hypervisor [21], widely used as the basis for several commercial and open source applications, mainly in-volving server virtualization and recently applied in embedded appliances. In 2011, Xi et al. [22] proposed RT-Xen. Based on vanilla Xen, RT-Xen provided schedulers for supporting soft real-time applications. Currently, only the Real-Time De-ferrable Server (RTDS) has been kept in the last version of RT-Xen (v2.2). Anyway, RTDS was included also in vanilla Xen starting from v4.5. RT-Xen v2.2 supports both Earliest Dead-line First (EDF) and Rate Monotonic (RM) scheduling poli-cies, and it is possible to switch on the ﬂy between them; fur-ther, RT-Xen allows setting and getting scheduling parameters per-virtual CPUs (vCPUs). The RTDS scheduler assigns three parameters to every vCPUs, with a budget (the time allocated to a vCPU), a period (the period after which the budget can be reﬁlled), and extratime (whether a vCPU can still run af-ter budget expiration, when free physical CPU (pCPU) is avail-able). When a vCPU starts running on a pCPU, its execution is not necessarily continuous. This means that its budget can be spent anytime during the period. A vCPU can execute if there is a free pCPU, or if it is running a vCPU with a lower priority.
The deadline corresponds with the end of the period. RTDS can group pCPUs in CPU pools and assigns each domain (i.e., VM) into one of these pools. For each CPU pool, RTDS keeps two queues: a global runqueue which holds all the CPUs with a non-0 residual budget sorted by priority, and a depleted queue, which holds all the CPUs that used up their budget.
2) PREEMPT RT Linux: In the proposed PoC, we choose Linux as guest OS since it brings several advantages, like accessible and portable source code, in-depth research in the industrial ﬁeld, creating a strong alternative also in embedded environments [23]. The Linux Foundation supported several collaborative projects in the context of the real-time domain, developing the well-known PREEMPT RT patch [24]. This patch adds two more levels of preemption to the vanilla kernel, the Preemptible Kernel (Basic RT) and the Fully Preemptible Kernel options, in addition to the three levels provided by default. Further, PREEMPT RT removes most of the non-preemptible spinlocks, replaces sleeping mutexes with rt mutex type that implements priority inheritance, and implements a new version of the high-resolution timers. The SCHED FIFO, SCHED RR (round-robin), and the SCHED DEADLINE (implementation of the Earliest Deadline First (EDF)) are the real-time scheduler policies implemented in Linux. For both SCHED RR and SCHED FIFO the user needs to statically assign priorities.
Instead, SCHED DEADLINE leverages runtime, period, and deadline parameters to schedule tasks. SCHED DEADLINE allocates to a task runtime µs of execution time every T µs speciﬁed with the period. This allocated time is available within the speciﬁed deadline from the beginning of the period.
B. Temporal Isolation Assessment In the context of virtualization, temporal isolation is the ability to isolate or limit the impact of resource consumption (e.g. CPU, network, disk) of a VM on the performance degra-dation of other VMs and even against the host. This means that a critical task running in a VM must not cause delays to other critical and non-critical tasks running in different VMs, avoiding phenomena such as starvation, reduced throughput, and increased latency. Indeed, we need to take into account several knobs, e.g., guest OSes schedulers, vCPUs/pCPUs mapping, hypervisor scheduler, and so on: if not properly managed they could easily break temporal isolation.
In this work in progress paper, we highlight the need of per-forming systematic experiments to unveil potential interference under corner case conditions (e.g., stressful privileged/unpriv-ileged VMs, faults in the hypervisor, bad conﬁgurations, etc.).
The ultimate objective is twofold: i) quantifying how strong is the temporal isolation assured by the hypervisor, and ii) pro-viding guidelines for practitioners to ﬁne-tune the system pa-rameters in case of weak isolation. According to EN50128, we identiﬁed, among others, critical requirements like D.45 Re-sponse Timing and Memory Constraints, D.3 Avalanche/Stress Testing, and D.25 SEEA – Software Error Effect Analysis that should be considered to provide proper temporal isolation, even in lower SIL levels. The main idea is to leverage the well-known DoE to rigorously assess the impact and signiﬁcance of system parameters in different operational scenarios.
III. PRELIMINARY RESULTS At the current state of the work, we assess temporal isolation by implementing a stress VM, with different conﬁgurations, that runs side-by-side with replicas VMs, voter VM, and pVM depicted in Figure 2. For the sake of simplicity, the voter is implemented naively, i.e., it receives measures from replicas and just compare without alerting replicas. Further, the purpose of the stress VM is to cause a high computational load that likely results in interference between the existing VMs, in order to comply with the D.3 Avalanche/Stress Testing EN50128 requirement. We leveraged DoE to perform experiments to precisely analyzed what is the degree of induced interference (e.g., increasing variance of latencies) for both different stress VM vCPU/pCPU mappings and guest OSes real-time scheduler policies, by ﬁxing the Xen RTDS parameters. The PoC is preliminarily deployed on a hardware platform with 8 pCPUs Intel(R) Xeon(R) E5-2667, 16GB RAM, 200GB HDD, using Xen v4.13 as the hypervisor. We set up Xen RTDS scheduler with the default parameters, i.e., 4000µs for budget and 10000µs for the period, and set the vCPU/pCPU mappings for the pVM (i.e., Xen Dom0), replicas VM, voter VM, and stress VM as described in the following: • pVM: 2 vCPU pinned on pCPU0 and pCPU1; • voter VM: 2 vCPU pinned on physical pCPU2 and pCPU3; • replicas VM: 1 vCPUs pinned respectively on the pCPU4 and pCPU5; • stress VM: it can freely use the pCPU6 and pCPU7 as described in the next.
The idea behind the vCPU/pCPU conﬁguration for the stress VM is to consider 3 load levels, i.e., Low, Mid, and High. In particular: 1) Low, includes only 1 vCPU allocated to the stress VM, and it is pinned on one of the free pCPUs.
2) Mid, includes 4 vCPUs allocated to the stress VM.
Speciﬁcally, 2 vCPUs are pinned on the 2 free pCPU, while the other 2 vCPUs are pinned on the pCPU0 and pCPU1. In this way, the stress VM will use the pCPUs already allocated to the pVM, and will not interfere with the execution of the replicas and voter VMs.
3) High, includes 4 vCPUs allocated to the stress VM, and all of them are pinned on the pCPUs used by the replicas and the voter. In this scenario, we are TABLE I RESULTS FOR TESTED CONFIGURATIONS.

The other parameter on which we can operate is the sched-uler policy for the guest OSes used for replicas and the voter VMs. In these tests, we set VMs only with the SCHED FIFO policy. Hence, our test plan contemplates two factors, i.e., the Stress load and the guest OS Scheduler, with three and one levels respectively. This means that a full factorial Design of Experiment (DoE) establishes 3 experiments to be performed.
For each conﬁguration, we set N = 35 measurements that each replica send to the voter both w/ stress and w/o stress scenarios. For each experiment, TABLE I shows the results in terms of the average and standard deviation of latencies obtained in the scenario without the stress workload, and the increase of the same metrics when the stress workload is acti-vated. Further, in order to understand if the difference between the latency distributions obtained in both w/o and w/ scenarios is statistically signiﬁcant, we use the t-test by showing the obtained p-value. We set a p-value threshold equal to 0.05 to consider the two distributions statistically different or not.
As we expected, preliminary results show that the vCPU/pCPU mapping is a highly signiﬁcant factor for temporal interference since exists a non-negligible increase in the average latencies and standard deviation in scenarios with stress. For interlocking systems, there is no standard agreement on performance requirements in Europe, and each railway infrastructure can adopt its own thresholds.
For example, in [25] the requirement for acceptable voting response time is between 350ms and 500ms. Despite the obtained results appearing to be better according to the abovementioned thresholds, the voting logic adopted in this preliminary work is not representative of real operational conditions; rather, the most critical point to take into account is the high variability of these latency times. In future work, we planned another set of experiments to understand if different conﬁgurations of the hypervisor scheduler can mitigate temporal interference, even under stressful conditions.
IV. RELATED WORK PikeOS [26] is a commercial hypervisor from SYSGO, used also in the railway domain. PikeOS supports multi-core platforms and its architecture is based on the L4 microkernel.
PikeOS has been the target and the basis of several academic and industrial evaluations. Regarding certiﬁcation and formal veriﬁcation, in [27] the authors formalized the hardware-independent security-relevant part of PikeOS to prove intransitive noninterference properties [28]; moreover, in [29] the authors presented ﬁrst results in the veriﬁcation of the PikeOS microkernel system calls. Jailhouse [30] is a Linux-based partitioning hypervisor developed by Siemens, enabling AMP applications to cooperate with the Linux kernel to run bare-metal applications or properly conﬁgured guest OSes.
The main purpose is to enhance isolation rather than provide classic virtualization; thus, the hypervisor splits CPUs, memory, I/O ports, PCI devices, etc., into cells, i.e., strongly isolated domains, each of them assigned to one guest OS, and its applications, called inmates. Recently, in the context of the Hercules H2020 project, page coloring support has been added to Jailhouse, showing promising results about cache isolation.
However, temporal isolation evidence is not documented.
Similarly, Bao [31] is a lightweight bare-metal partitioning hypervisor, designed ad-hoc for mixed-criticality IoT systems.
Bao focuses on security and safety requirements by providing strong isolation, fault-containment, real-time features, and im-plements page coloring [32]. Bao has been recently ported to Xilinx’s ZCU104 MPSoC, showing reduced overheads while keeping low partition interference. Xtratum [33] is a para-virtualized partitioning hypervisor for the avionic domain, built according to the ARINC 653 standard. Xtratum supports several CPU families (e.g., Intel, Leon, ARM), providing strong temporal isolation between virtual partitions by exploit-ing a ﬁxed cyclic scheduler. Spatial separation is guaranteed by imposing partitions allocated statically at different physical memory addresses, with no memory areas shared between partitions. Xtratum deﬁnes a minimum set of deterministic hypercalls and enables interrupts only for currently running partitions, to minimize temporal interference. Cache coherence is guaranteed by setting memory areas as non-cacheable in the virtual memory map, unless target platforms implement hard-ware virtualization features or cache coherency acceleration.
In this short paper, we focused on Xen since we are assisting a proliferation of projects that leverage it as a basis for safety-critical virtualized systems. Xen currently provides real-time support for scheduling (ARINC, RTDS, Null schedulers), a minimal size (less than 30KSLOC) for ARM-based hardware environments, paravirtual and GPU mediation for rich I/O, TEE virtualization support, and Dom0less architecture [19].
Xen is also gaining popularity in the automotive domain, thanks to vertical initiatives like the Automotive Grade Linux (AG according to ISO 26262 [34]. Finally, Xen fully supports cloud computing infrastructures, providing mechanisms that include migration, balancing, and high availability. Thus, it can easily support potential solutions for orchestrating mixed-criticality scenarios like RSaaS, by running RTOSes and GPOSes consolidated on the same hardware platform.
In that direction, Xilinx is currently developing a lightweight solution called RunX, which exploits Xen to both run containers as VMs in the context of the industrial IoT and edge devices, which often require assuring real-time behavior [35]. It is worth noting that the problem of time partitioning is still left exposed for multi/many cores architecture.
V. CONCLUSION AND FUTURE PLAN In this short paper, we presented ongoing research on using a real-time ﬂavor of general-purpose hypervisors for orches-trating virtualized signaling railway systems. In particular, we highlighted the need for a methodology intending to evaluate temporal isolation property for certiﬁcation purposes. The pro-posal includes the use of DoE for planning experiments to i) properly quantify isolation provided by the chosen hypervisor and ii) providing guidelines to carefully tuning crucial param-eters like guest OS and hypervisor schedulers, vCPU/pCPU mapping, etc. These, are some main levers on which acting to mitigate temporal interference. Future plans include applying the proposed approach against other conﬁgurations of Xen, like using partitioning (i.e., the null scheduler) and Dom0-less features, and using different real-time communication approaches (e.g., XDP [36]) for unprivileged domains.

Compared to spatial isolation, which is often guaranteed by only using hardware-assisted mechanisms (e.g., MMU), temporal isolation remains a critical and open research problem, "We highlight the need for a systematic evaluation of the temporal isolation to demonstrate the feasibility of using general-purpose hypervisors in the safety-critical context for certification purposes.", "Preliminary results show that the vCPU/pCPU mapping is a highly significant factor for temporal interference since exists a non-negligible increase in the average latencies and standard deviation in scenarios with stress.", "The proposal includes the use of DoE for planning experiments to i) properly quantify isolation provided by the chosen hypervisor and ii) providing guidelines to carefully tuning crucial parameters like guest OS and hypervisor schedulers, vCPU/pCPU mapping, etc.", "For interlocking systems, there is no standard agreement on performance requirements in Europe, and each railway infrastructure can adopt its own thresholds."

This academic paper (arXiv:2208.14109v1, Aug 2022) by Cotroneo, De Simone, and Natella from Università degli Studi di Napoli Federico II investigates temporal isolation assessment in virtualized Railway Signaling as a Service (RSaaS) systems. The paper proposes using the real-time flavor of the Xen hypervisor and PREEMPT RT-patched Linux guests to build virtualized railway signaling systems that consolidate mixed-criticality functions.

**Key Points:**

- **Motivation:** Railway signaling systems are increasingly adopting cloud and virtualization to reduce costs and enable remote control, but assessing temporal isolation is critical for safety standards like EN50128. Spatial isolation (e.g., via MMU) is easier to guarantee, but temporal isolation remains an open research problem.

- **Proposed System (PoC):** A 2oo2 (two-out-of-two) fault-tolerant architecture with 3 unprivileged VMs—two replicas simulating sensors and one voter—plus a privileged VM (Dom0), running on Xen with RTDS scheduler.

- **Methodology:** The authors advocate using Design of Experiments (DoE) to systematically evaluate temporal isolation factors such as vCPU/pCPU mapping, hypervisor scheduler parameters, and guest OS scheduler policies.

- **Preliminary Results:** Experiments with a stress VM at Low, Mid, and High load levels showed significant increases in average latency and standard deviation (up to ~109% and ~1806% increases respectively) for replicas and voter VMs under stress, with t-test p-values well below 0.05, confirming statistical significance. vCPU/pCPU mapping was identified as a highly significant factor for temporal interference.

- **Related Work:** The paper reviews other hypervisors (PikeOS, Jailhouse, Bao, Xtratum) but focuses on Xen due to its real-time scheduling support, small footprint, and cloud computing capabilities.

- **Conclusion:** The paper calls for systematic temporal isolation assessment to provide evidence for certification, with future work planned on different Xen configurations (null scheduler, Dom0less) and real-time communication approaches (XDP).
