Hyperlinks are provided for a direct access to additional information, when relevant. The SERA is the Single European Railway Area defined by the Directive 2012/34/EU, as the railway system of the European Union. Railway systems which are part of the SERA are bound by the technical requirements of the Interoperability Directive (EU) 2016/797 and of the Safety Directive (EU) 2016/798 and by the relevant Commission Regulations on the so-called TSI, Technical Specifications for Interoperability. Urban rail systems have been jointly defined by UITP and UNIFE through their common Urban Rail Platform in 2023 (see 202309_URP_definition of urban rail.pdf). Some urban rail systems are part of the SERA and fall in the scope of the TSI, and most of them are excluded from the SERA. Among the non-SERA rail systems, two sub-categories are very specific and often presented as UGT or UGTS (Urban Guided Transit systems), namely Metro systems, fully separated from any other traffic, and Tram or Light Rail systems, which are also road systems and thus shall be potentially regarded along with other road-borne public transport systems (bus, etc.). More details are provided in the section DEFINITION below. Non-SERA urban rail systems are, most often, excluded from the scope of EU Legislation. This document highlights outcomes of research projects along with a review of standards and technical specifications, identifying those which might be used for non-SERA urban rail systems, at the convenience of relevant local stakeholders (public transport authorities, operators, manufacturers), depending on the local regulatory framework applicable. January 2025 4 SAFETY The Safety rules applied for Acceptance, Approval and Certification – AAC – of the systems follow these principles: • The authorisation for putting a local rail system into service usually involves national authorities, with AAC rules depending on national and local situations. Safety requirements follow different principles among Member States, e.g. GAME in France, ALARP in UK, individual responsibility in Germany (Betriebsleiter). • The competent public authorities are free to decide whether they should apply or not some SERA specifications or some EU standards or adopt functional or technical requirements specific to the local situation. The Safety rules applicable to non-SERA rail systems in Europe have been studied and harmonised within the EU Research project MODSAFE (2007-2013) and are still valid1. AAC Safety specifications are presented in Chapter 1 together with updated standards which might be used. SECURITY AND CYBERSECURITY On Security and Cybersecurity, this report similarly focuses on the very numerous standards and specifications that could apply to non-SERA rail systems (or sub-systems or components), detailed in the relevant section 2.2. • A lot of work has been achieved over the past 20 years, addressing initially issues of security – mainly focusing on terrorist attacks. 1 See UITP MyLibrary - Documents : MODSafe - Modular Urban Transport Safety and Security Analysis (completed) - (accreditation required). As regard Safety, the present document targets non-SERA urban rail systems, which include metro and tram/Light Rail systems, as well as the urban, suburban, regional rail systems declared by each of the 27 EU Member States as functionally separate from the SERA. The non-SERA rail systems do not depend on any European rail technical legislation. They have to apply national or even regional rules throughout the lifetime of the systems. Decision makers determining the technical requirements attached to each non-SERA local rail system are national and mostly competent local public authorities, since the services to customers are not commercially viable and are operated under Public Service Obligations (PSO), regulated at EU level by the PSO Regulation (EC) 1370/2007. January 2025 5 • Cybersecurity has been a rising concern and is already covered by many specifications also mentioned in section 2.2. The current focus to frame cybersecurity is mainly on the IEC 63452 standard, currently under revision. Applicability of IEC 63452 standard for non-SERA urban rail systems is of voluntary application, unless otherwise specified at local national level. In addition, it is important to note that some recent EU legislation might apply to non-SERA rail systems, and the extent to which it might apply to the non-SERA rail systems is under clarification. These legislations are as follows: Critical infrastructure (CER Directive2) An EU legislation called CER Directive might apply to some categories of Urban rail systems regarded as “critical infrastructure”. For the European Union institutions, these systems are critical when they cross at least a border. However, when transposing the directive, some Member States decided to designate some local public transport systems as critical infrastructure within their country. The protection of European critical infrastructure in the energy and transport sectors has been originally regulated by Council Directive 2008/114/EC on the identification and designation of European critical infrastructures and the assessment of the need to improve their protection. This directive has been repealed in 2022 by Directive (EU) 2022/2557 (CER Directive) on the resilience of critical entities. ENISA Regulation The European Union Agency for Cybersecurity (ENISA) has been created in 2004 to contribute to a high level of network and information security within the Union, to raise awareness of network and information security and to develop and promote a culture of network and information security in society for the benefit of citizens, consumers, enterprises and public sector organisations in the Union. The latest Regulation (EU) 2019/881 on ENISA notably lays down a framework for the establishment of European cybersecurity certification schemes for the purpose of ensuring an adequate level of cybersecurity for ICT (information and Communication technologies) products, ICT services and ICT processes in the Union, as well as for the purpose of avoiding the fragmentation of the internal market with regard to cybersecurity certification schemes in the Union. Scope of this Regulation (EU) 2019/881 is cross-sectorial and thus shall apply to ICT in urban rail systems. Security of network and information systems (NIS2 Directive) The security of network and information systems across the European Union, with a focus on cyber-related threats, was assured since 2016 through Directive (EU) 2016/1148 (NIS Directive) of the European Parliament and Council, which establishes measures to ensure a high common level of security of network and information systems across the Union. 2 CER: Critical Entities Resilience. January 2025 6 This Directive has been repealed in 2022 by Directive (EU) 2022/2555 (NIS2 Directive) on measures for a high common level of cybersecurity across the Union3. NIS2 requires organisations across different sectors to ensure that networks and systems they use to deliver services and conduct their activities attain a higher level of cybersecurity, and that essential and important entities within the scope, such as cloud providers and public administration entities, take appropriate and proportionate technical, operational and organisational cybersecurity measures. This includes, among others, a requirement to ensure security in network and information systems acquisition, development and maintenance, including vulnerability handling and disclosure. The Directive requires the Commission to adopt implementing acts for certain types of entities, laying down the technical and the methodological requirements, as well as sectoral requirements. One of these act is the CRA Implementing act (see below). Another Directive (DORA)4 defines rules applicable for digital operational resilience for the financial sector. Cybersecurity requirements for hardware and software products (CRA) The Cyber Resilience Act (CRA)5 is currently (as of Nov 2024) under adoption process and intends to amend Regulation (EU) 2019/1020 on market surveillance and compliance of products. The CRA sets out cybersecurity requirements for hardware and software products placed on the EU market, in order to: • Create conditions for the development of secure products with digital elements by ensuring that hardware and software products are placed on the market with fewer vulnerabilities (thanks to a coherent cybersecurity framework, facilitating compliance for hardware and software producers) and ensure that manufacturers take security seriously throughout a product’s life cycle since the design and development phase. • Create conditions which allow users to take cybersecurity into account when selecting and using products with digital elements, by enhancing the transparency of security properties of products with digital elements and enabling businesses and consumers to use these products securely. 3 NIS2 Directive is also amending e-IDAS Regulation (EU) 910/2014 and Directive (EU) 2018/1972 (European Electronic Communications Code). 4 Regulation (EU) 2022/2554 on digital operational resilience for the financial sector. 5 COM/2022/454 final (CRA – Cyber Resilience Act) on horizontal cybersecurity requirements for products with digital elements and amending Regulation (EU) 2019/1020. January 2025 7 GENERAL PRINCIPLES AND DEFINITIONS GENERAL PRINCIPLES The Safety Directive (EU) 2016/798 does not apply to non-SERA rail systems and TSI (Technical Specifications for Interoperability) requirements regarding the safety of the SERA systems, such as Common Safety Method (CSM), Common Safety Targets (CST), Conformity Assessment, are not appropriate for non-SERA urban rail systems which are out of their scope. Acceptance, Approval and Certification (AAC) of any non-SERA urban rail system are the responsibility of national, regional, local relevant public authorities, depending on each local situation. Any harmonisation at the European level has to be developed without prejudice to the competence of these authorities in each European country. Security and cybersecurity should follow the same principles, although some transverse issues can cover several local public transport modes together (e.g. including bus). Many standards, or de-facto standards, dealing with Safety, Security and Cyber Security may however be used on a voluntary basis by non-SERA rail systems decision-makers, after a clear distribution of responsibilities for their implementation (design, construction and operation, including funding and financing). DEFINITIONS AAC Acceptance, Approval and Certification AOM Autorité Organisatrice de Mobilité (competent authority for local passenger public transport in France) Cybersecurity means the activities necessary to protect network and information systems, the users of such systems, and other persons affected by cyber threats (see Regulation 2019/881 on ENISA, article 2(1)). Cyber threat means any potential circumstance, event or action that could damage, disrupt or otherwise adversely impact network and information systems, the users of such systems and other persons (see Regulation 2019/881 on ENISA, article 2(8)). EAM Elementary Activity Modules Harm Injury or damage to the health of people, or damage to property or the environment. Hazard An unintentional event or physical condition that has the potential to cause fatalities, injuries, property damage, infrastructure damage, agricultural loss, damage to the environment, interruption of business, or other types of harm or loss. For the purposes of MODSAFE, hazard is the term referring to safety scenarios. See also Threat. January 2025 8 ICT Information and Communication Technologies Physical security The part of security concerned with measures and concepts designed to (1) safeguard personnel6; (2) prevent unauthorized access to equipment, installations, materiel, and documents; and (3) safeguard equipment, installations, materiel, and documents against espionage, sabotage, damage, and theft. Safety Freedom from unacceptable levels of risks resulting from unintentional acts or circumstances. Security Freedom from unacceptable levels of risks resulting from intentional acts or circumstance. See also Physical security. Threat7 A potential action or situation that may cause harm to the infrastructure or its occupants. TSI Technical Specification for Interoperability (see below) Urban Transport Security (UTS) UTS is the integrated security of any urban public transport system inclusive of transport security, personnel security, property security and cyber security, in cooperation with external security service providers (police services, private companies, etc.). Vulnerability The gap between protective measures safeguarding a given system and identified risks. Vulnerability is a measure of the likelihood that various types of safeguards against threat scenarios will fail8. COMPLEMENTARY INFORMATION The TSI define the technical and operational standards which must be met by each subsystem or part of subsystem belonging to the SERA in order to meet the essential requirements and to ensure the interoperability and safety of the EU railway system. The essential requirements are targeting safety, reliability and availability, health, environmental protection, technical compatibility and accessibility. Several TSI are related to safety, and the next revision of the TSI shall also address security and cybersecurity. Among the non-SERA rail systems, two sub-categories are very specific and often presented as UGT or UGTS (Urban Guided Transit systems): • Metro systems are urban rail systems typically operated on a dedicated infrastructure (including underground, elevated or surface sections) and independent from any other traffic (road, rail or pedestrian). 6 Note that Personnel security is a different issue. See: Personnel Security - an overview | ScienceDirect Topics. 7 Threats are distinct from hazards because they are not acts of nature, accidents, or organic happenstances for which tunnels are normally designed. Rather, threats are typically characterised as acts of intrusion; placement of explosive devices; and/or chemical, biological, or radiological attacks. In the case of terrorism, a threat consists of a scenario that combines a weapon, a perpetrator, or aggressor, a delivery mode, and tactics (path of approach, use of stealth or force). While hazards are associated with safety, threats are associated with security (see also Hazard). 8 Any feature or characteristic of the design, or operation of a critical component, that could be exploited by a threat to disrupt or to destroy. The vulnerability of a given system generally increases with dependency. January 2025 9 • Tram systems are urban rail systems operated on infrastructure shared with road traffic (including pedestrian areas), or partially on separate infrastructure. For tram systems having sections segregated from road traffic the term Light Rail System (LRS) may be used. Both sub-categories are covering systems which are designed on the basis of purely local functional requirements, taking into account that: • Metro systems are very often automated, up to so-called “driverless” systems. The “GOA4”9 systems are driven by ATC (Automated Train Control) control-command sub-systems including ATP (Automatic Train Protection), ATO (Automatic Train Operation) and ATS (Automatic Train Supervision). In comparison with the SERA rail systems, the ATP Functional Requirements Specifications – FRS - and System Requirements Specifications – SRS – are based on different approaches, the ATO FRS and SRS are coming from metro experience, and the ATS does not apply to the SERA10. In addition automated systems operated with Communication Based Train Control-command – CBTC – are following in terms of use of the Spectrum the EC Implementing Decision (EU) 2020/1426 of ECC Decision (08)01 on ITS – Intelligent Transport Systems – and EC Implementing Decision (EU) 2021/1067 of ECC Decision (20)01 on WAS/RLAN – Wireless Access Systems/Radio Local Area Networks. • Tram/Light Rail systems are driven on-sight, and are not only rail-guided systems, but road systems in terms of operation. Regarding the Spectrum use, they are regarded (and bus systems as well) as part of Road ITS in terms of application of above decisions on ITS. Therefore tram/ Light Rail and bus are in many cases to be considered jointly. 9 GOA: Grade of Automation. 10 In the future, ATS may be introduced in some isolated areas, such as ports for freight or workshops and garages for freight and passengers. January 2025 10 1. SAFETY 1.1. SAFETY ASSESSMENT FROM MODSAFE OUTCOMES AND RELEVANT STANDARDS (UPDATED) MODSAFE outcomes convinced the European Commission that harmonising AAC procedures across Europe was not useful, although cross-acceptance could be promoted. The project contributed to the exclusion of the non-SERA urban rail systems from the scope of the (Rail) Interoperability Directive11 and the (Rail) Safety Directive12. The deliverables of the MODSAFE project which are still valid for safety assessment are: • MODSAFE D7.1 Review of current AAC procedures. It describes the national rules and actors involved and their responsibilities in each EU Member State for the AACs of non-SERA urban rail systems at different stages of their life cycle. The report shows the diversity of situations. • MODSAFE D7.3 Typical AAC model. It splits projects over their life cycle into Elementary Activity Modules - EAM - and proposes a reference model (called Generic AAC Procedure) building upon use cases of: France, Germany, Hungary, Sweden and UK (for LUL). • MODSAFE D7.4 Proposal for a generic AAC Process (guidance for a case-by-case adaptation). It recommends how responsibilities should be split between the various actors for the various Elementary Activity Modules, with flexibility for each EAM. It is a guide for national/local decision-makers intending to implement a new project (e.g. for a metro in a city that does not yet have one). These deliverables are available for download on the UITP website (accreditation required), with selected extracts provided below. The document also explores the relationship between established standards and areas that remain unstandardised. 1.2. PUTTING-INTO-SERVICE SAFETY-CRITICAL NON-SERA URBAN RAIL SYSTEMS (UPDATED) The process of putting-into-service safety-critical non-SERA urban rail systems is a complex, multiplayer process, where different actors have different roles and tasks. From a wider point of view, the diversity of these processes in different countries also increases the complexity of AAC process. The aim of these processes is to guarantee that the system installed fulfils certain requirements, among which: • Functional requirements specifying what the system has to achieve. 11 Directive (EU) 2016/797 Rail Interoperability Directive, amended by the Artificial Intelligence Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689) and supplemented by Decision (EU) 2017/1474. 12 Directive (EU) 2016/798 Rail Safety Directive, on railway safety. January 2025 11 • Technical requirements which constrain the developer in subsequent activities in the life cycle. • Goals which guide the developer where choice exists. • References to data used by the proposed system. • Design or implementation advice. Safety requirements may appear as an individual requirement class or as a part of the functional and non-functional requirements. The fulfillment of different requirements can be checked by different parties during the life cycle of the system. The different parties have different interest in this process, different expertise and knowledge on the system. This is a pre-requisite of the guarantee of independence. CENELEC EN 50126 standard and its accompanying suite of standards mentioned in the table below are widely accepted as reference standards that can be used for any kind of railway system – SERA and non-SERA. EN 50126-1: 2017/FprA1: 2024 The Specification and Demonstration of Reliability, Availability, Maintainability and Safety (RAMS) - Part 1: Generic RAMS Process EN 50126-2: 2017/FprA1: 2024 The Specification and Demonstration of Reliability, Availability, Maintainability and Safety (RAMS) - Part 2: Systems Approach to Safety EN 50129: 2018 Communications, signalling and processing systems - Safety related electronic systems for signalling EN 50129: 2018/AC: 2019-04 Communications, signalling and processing systems - Safety related electronic systems for signalling prEN 50129: 2023 Railway Application - Communication, signalling and processing system - Safety related electronic systems for signalling EN 50716: 2023 Railway Applications - Requirements for software development (Supersedes EN 50128 and EN 50 657) Table 1 - CENELEC EN 50126 and Accompanying Standards The main participants of this process are: • Supervisory authority, which licenses the operation of the system. • Customer and operator of the system (for example, a transportation company). • Contractor; developer and manufacturer industry. • Safety assessor, independent expert, if required. January 2025 12 Figure 1 - Participants of the Safety Process For instance, the transportation company fixes its requirements on a new system or equipment in a customer statement of requirements. In many cases this document has to be approved by the supervisory authority, and this is the basis for the developer to elaborate the company-specific system specification. This system specification is the starting point of the system development. According to the regulation of several European countries, before the installation, the documentation of system and the equipment itself must be examined by an expert. A positive report is a precondition to receive the operation license from the supervisory authority. The management of the transportation companies, particularly the safety management, is supported in many cases by a safety organisation, which coordinates and carries out the tasks of the safety process from the viewpoint of the transportation company. Similarly, the developer has an internal safety organisation responsible for ensuring the safety of the delivered system and verifying that all specified safety requirements are met. Keeping the level of risk in the transportation processes as low as possible is primarily the responsibility of the transportation companies, particularly in case of mass transit. Therefore, it is desirable that the management of the transportation system can prove that the required level of safety for the transportation process is achieved. The setting and agreement of the safety target is often the task of some authority, which is competent in safety issues. Certification is the process of issuing a certificate to indicate conformance with specified requirements. Certification is generally an activity whereby a designated body, independent of the involved entities, gives a written assurance that a product, process or service conforms to specified requirements. In fact, any organisation or individual may issue a certificate, and its importance will clearly vary with its nature and its issuing body. For non-SERA urban rail systems certification is not necessarily required and the organisations which allow the operation also to vary from country to country. In order to achieve certification, the developer of a safety-related product must convince the appropriate regulator of its safety. Given the abstract nature of safety, this is invariably a difficult task. The developer must be able to show that all important hazards have been identified and dealt with, and that the integrity of the system is appropriate for the application. Certification may also require evidence of compliance with some particular standard, although such compliance is not in itself sufficient proof of the appropriateness of the design. The developer will need to Supervisory authority Contractor Customer Safety assessor January 2025 13 provide extensive evidence of the development methods used, and the testing performed to investigate the system's behaviour. In addition, it will be necessary to produce a rigorous argument to support the claim that the system is sufficiently safe, and that it will remain so throughout its life. The work involved in achieving certification is considerable and requires careful planning. 1.3. LIFE CYCLE APPROACH The life cycle approach to be considered is described in Figure 2 below. It applies to the overall urban rail system including all technical sub-systems as well as operations and maintenance aspects. Life cycle phases 1 to 4 are under the responsibility of the Operator and/or of the competent public transport authority to specify the requirements of the greenfield or brownfield non-SERA urban rail project. Life cycle phases 5 to 9 are under the responsibility of the Supplier to build the system as specified: this includes the Supplier validation and acceptance of the system. Life cycle phase 10 covers and ends with the Safety Authority’s licensing for the commercial operation of the project. Life cycle phases 11 to 14 are under the obligation of the Operator as part of the public service contract signed with the competent public transport authority. They cover the operations and maintenance of the project including performance monitoring and potential modification and retrofit, up to the potential decommissioning and disposal. Figure 2 - Life Cycle Approach January 2025 14 1.4. DESCRIPTION OF A GENERIC AAC PROCEDURE FOR NON-SERA RAIL SYSTEMS 1.4.1. Description of a generic process for Safety management A specific outcome of MODSAFE is the definition of a generic process for Safety management which identifies Elementary Activity Modules - EAMs - organised according to three hierarchical levels as follows: • System level • Level of functionality • Level of safety For each of them, a process has been defined (the two first are not presented here). The figure below presents the generic process at the level of safety. On the figure, the darker background colour of the boxes indicates the EAMs, while boxes with lighter background colours show connecting processes or documentations, which are inputs and outputs for EAMs. Safety requirements can be defined based on the functions of a system, using a hazard and risk analysis. In case of safety requirements there is a strong need to check, whether the safety requirements were defined in an appropriate way and the results are acceptable. The agreed safety requirement specification is a clear basis for later design and implementation phases, as it determines system architecture properties as well as the methods that shall be used during the development. The supplier of the system has to demonstrate that the safety requirements are met. This demonstration or justification must be usually assessed before it can be stated that all safety requirements are fulfilled. The Independent Safety Assessment follows the whole development process, and can result in an assessment report, which can be used in course of system approval. This document, published January 2025 by UITP, provides technical specifications on safety, security, and cybersecurity for non-SERA (Single European Railway Area) urban rail systems in the European Union. It serves as a roadmap to facilitate decision-making for stakeholders in building their own safety, security, and cybersecurity policies.

**Key Context:** Non-SERA urban rail systems (metros, trams/Light Rail) are excluded from EU Safety and Interoperability Directives, meaning they are subject to national/local rules rather than EU legislation. The document identifies standards and specifications that can be used voluntarily by local stakeholders.

**Safety (Section 1):** Safety rules for Acceptance, Approval, and Certification (AAC) depend on national/local situations. The MODSAFE research project (2007-2013) remains the foundation, providing a generic AAC process with Elementary Activity Modules (EAMs). Key participants include: Operator, Supplier, Authority, and Independent Safety Assessor/Certification Body. The CENELEC EN 50126 standard suite is widely accepted for both SERA and non-SERA systems. A life cycle approach (14 phases) is recommended, covering specification, design, construction, operation, and decommissioning. Factors influencing AAC include system size, complexity, required Safety Integrity Level (SIL), project nature, Grade of Automation (GOA), and system category (tram vs. metro).

**Security and Cybersecurity (Section 2):** The document reviews numerous standards and specifications for security (focusing on terrorist attacks) and cybersecurity (growing concern, notably IEC 63452 standard under revision). It highlights that several recent EU legislations may apply to non-SERA rail systems:
- **CER Directive (EU 2022/2557):** Critical infrastructure resilience, may apply when systems cross borders or are designated by Member States.
- **ENISA Regulation (EU 2019/881):** Establishes European cybersecurity certification schemes for ICT products/services.
- **NIS2 Directive (EU 2022/2555):** Requires higher cybersecurity levels for network and information systems across sectors.
- **Cyber Resilience Act (CRA):** Under adoption, sets cybersecurity requirements for hardware/software products placed on the EU market.

The document defines key terms such as Safety, Security, Physical Security, Cybersecurity, Threat, Hazard, and Vulnerability. It also provides detailed qualification criteria for Inspection Bodies (ISO/IEC 17020), Certification Bodies (ISO/IEC 17065), and Independent Safety Assessors (EN 50129).

# 5th ENISA-ERA Conference on Cybersecurity in Railways

Breadcrumb

[Back to Events](https://www.enisa.europa.eu/events)

conference Dec 01 TO 02, 2025 from 9:00am to 2:00pm (Europe/Tallinn)

Registration for this conference is now closed. Thank you for your understanding.

The European Union Agency for Cybersecurity (ENISA) and the [European Union Agency for Railways (ERA)](https://www.era.europa.eu/), with the support of [Estonian Railways](https://www.evr.ee/en), are pleased to announce the 5th edition of the Cybersecurity in Railways conference, the annual event dedicated to exploring the latest advancements, best practices, and challenges in the field of cybersecurity in the railway sector.

The 2025 edition, that will take place in Tallinn, Estonia, on 1-2 December, will bring together cybersecurity professionals, researchers, industry experts, government officials, and practitioners to exchange knowledge, insights, and experiences.

This event is the continuation of the close collaboration between ERA and ENISA on cybersecurity in the railway domain.

This year, the location of the conference is moving away from the traditional Lille and Athens to get closer to the implementation of railway cybersecurity projects. The support of Estonian Railways is the first step in supporting the cyber rail community with their local priorities.

The topics of this joint event, together with the strong support from the European Commission, will cover:

* Opening with a focus on regional challenges/initiatives
* Cybersecurity policy updates: NIS2 directive, CRA regulation, European Commission request for TSI updates
* Capacity building and training for the railway sector
* Feedback from railway cybersecurity projects: national implementations, sector initiatives

As every year, the conference will keep on providing networking opportunities, aiming at building a railway cybersecurity community. Speakers and participants will share information on the latest developments and raise awareness among railway stakeholders about cybersecurity risks and mitigations.

ENISA, ERA and Estonian Railways are looking forward to welcoming you to Tallinn!

* Registration is free of charge and will be handled on a first-come, first-served basis;

# China High-Speed Rail and Rail Transit Equipment: Market Scale and Competitive Landscape 2026

2026-06-03 · 天下工厂产业研究院

![China High-Speed Rail and Rail Transit Equipment: Market Scale and Competitive Landscape 2026](https://ineq-seshat-research.oss-cn-beijing.aliyuncs.com/covers/c4344c0e41caf884.jpg)

Series[《China Key Industries 2026: Market & Competitive Landscape Deep-Dive Series》](/en/series/china-industry-deep-dive-2026)· Part 40 of 174[View full series →](/en/series/china-industry-deep-dive-2026)

China's high-speed rail story begins in 1993, when the average commercial operating speed of Chinese passenger trains was approximately 48 kilometers per hour.

The fastest passenger trains of that era were the "green carriages" — olive-painted cars running the Beijing-Shanghai, Beijing-Guangzhou, and Beijing-Harbin trunk lines. Their theoretical top speed was 120 km/h, but with poor track conditions and dense station stops, average speeds hovered around 50 km/h. Beijing to Shanghai took sixteen hours; Beijing to Guangzhou, thirty. Board the train and you would wake the next morning still on board.

More than thirty years later, on December 26, 2025, a new high-speed line from Xi'an to Yan'an opened, pushing China's total high-speed rail operating mileage past **50,000 kilometers** — exceeding the combined total of every other country on Earth. In the same year, Fuxing-series EMUs operated on the Whoosh Jakarta-Bandung high-speed railway in Indonesia at 350 km/h, compressing what had been a three-hour-plus journey to forty minutes. It was Southeast Asia's — and the entire Southern Hemisphere's — first true high-speed railway, and by the end of 2025 it had carried more than 13 million passengers across its first two years of operation.

A country whose fastest passenger train could not exceed 120 km/h in 1993, averaging less than 50 km/h nationally, had in under thirty years become a country commanding 70 percent of global high-speed rail mileage and capable of packaging an entire high-speed rail system for export. This is not merely an arithmetic problem in infrastructure construction speed — it is the ascent of a complete industrial ecosystem.

As of 2026, that story is turning a new page: domestic new-line construction is stabilizing, overseas markets are opening a second growth curve, early-deployed EMUs are entering their peak heavy-maintenance cycle, and aftermarket revenue is set to surge over this decade. China's rail transit equipment industry stands at a pivotal engine-switching moment.

## Executive Summary

This report systematically examines China's high-speed rail EMU and rail transit equipment industry — its market structure, supply chain, key company financials, and development outlook. Core findings:

**Market Size**: In 2025, China's rail transit equipment market reached approximately CNY 500 billion on a broad basis (rolling stock ~180 billion; components ~120 billion; signaling & control ~40 billion; maintenance ~80 billion; other engineering ~80 billion). As aftermarket maintenance enters its peak cycle, the broad-basis market is forecast to exceed CNY 650 billion by 2030.

**Competitive Landscape**: CRRC (601766) dominates domestically, with rail equipment revenue of CNY 123.6 billion and rolling stock market share exceeding 60%. China Railway Signal & Communication (688009) monopolizes railway signaling; CRRC Times Electric (688187) leads traction converters and power semiconductors. The supply chain is highly concentrated from upstream to downstream, with domestic substitution essentially complete.

**Growth Engines**: New-line construction has compressed from a peak of 3,000+ km/year to 800–1,000 km/year, but overseas orders are surging. CRRC's international new-order intake reached approximately CNY 65 billion in 2025, up ~~38% YoY — record-high. Whoosh (Indonesia), Laos-China, Hungary-Serbia, China-Thailand, and other projects continue advancing, with the Kyrgyzstan-Uzbekistan line entering preliminary construction. Aftermarket maintenance enters peak: approximately 400 EMU sets per year entering Level-5 overhaul, with 2024 aftermarket service revenue of ~CNY 41.8 billion (+~~25% YoY).

**Technology Frontier**: The CR450 EMU completed a record 453 km/h test, the fastest ever recorded for a high-speed train in commercial development, and is expected to achieve design finalization after completing 600,000 km of operational validation in 2026, targeting a commercial operating speed of 400 km/h. Hydrogen-powered EMUs, energy-storage EMUs, and fully autonomous operation are all accelerating toward validation.

**Risk Factors**: Compression in domestic new-line construction creates phased weakness in rolling stock demand; National Railway Group's debt burden constrains procurement timing; overseas projects face political risk and localization competition; export control escalation may affect key chip supply chains.

**Research Tool**: Researchers seeking to map the distribution and capacity of high-speed rail component suppliers can use a China-based factory database ([www.tianxiagongchang.com](http://www.tianxiagongchang.com)) to search for factories producing aluminum body sections, bogies, fasteners, contact-wire fittings, and other sub-categories. The platform indexes 4.8 million active manufacturing enterprises across China, filterable by province, city, and industry classification.

## Chapter I　Definitions and Classification: Speed Tiers, Product Spectrum, and Supply Chain Overview

### 1. Speed Tiers and Product Spectrum

China classifies rail transit equipment into five major categories: high-speed railway EMUs, inter-city railway EMUs, conventional railway locomotives and passenger coaches, urban rail vehicles (metro, light rail, suburban rail), and engineering/maintenance vehicles.

**High-Speed Railway EMUs (200–350+ km/h)**

This is the most technically demanding and highest unit-value product category in the industry. Within it, three speed tiers exist:

First tier: 200–250 km/h — represented by early CRH1/2/5 Hexie-series and the current CR300 series, primarily serving inter-city and regional high-speed corridors. Single-set capacity ranges from 500 to 600 passengers.

Second tier: 300–350 km/h — the absolute mainstream of China's high-speed trunk network. The Beijing-Shanghai, Beijing-Guangzhou, Shanghai-Kunming, and other core corridors operate at this tier. The Fuxing CR400AF (8-car) and CR400BF (16-car) are the flagship products, sustaining 350 km/h commercial operation with world-class ride quality and energy efficiency. The longest CR400 formation (17 cars) carries over 1,000 passengers per trip.

Third tier: 400 km/h and above — next-generation. The CR450 entered testing in 2024 and reached 453 km/h in limit tests on the Beijing-Shanghai HSR in 2025, setting a global record. It is currently undergoing operational validation, expected to achieve design finalization after completing 600,000 km in 2026, with a target commercial speed of 400 km/h.

**Urban Rail Vehicles**

Includes metro Type-A (3 m wide, highest capacity), Type-B (2.8 m), Type-C cars, light rail, trams, and suburban rail. China's urban rail network exceeds 10,000 km, covering 50+ cities.

**Conventional Railway Locomotives**

Electric and diesel locomotives are the primary traction force for freight railways. Demand is relatively stable, less correlated to new-line construction than passenger HSR.

**Engineering Vehicles and Special Equipment**

Track-laying machinery, tamping machines, catenary maintenance vehicles, inspection trains, and line maintenance machinery — a stable sub-segment that grows in tandem with network scale.

### 2. Supply Chain Overview

The HSR EMU supply chain comprises seven value-density layers from system integrator to base materials:

**Layer 1 — Vehicle Integration**: CRRC subsidiaries (Qingdao Sifang, Zhuzhou, Tangshan, Changchun) handle final assembly and integration testing. A standard HSR EMU set has a value of CNY 150–200 million.

**Layer 2 — Traction Systems**: Traction converters, traction motors, and main transformers. CRRC Times Electric (688187) supplies over 60% domestically, and is among a handful of global companies capable of mass-producing SiC power modules for HSR traction.

**Layer 3 — Train Control and Signaling**: ATP, ATC, CTCS equipment — dominated by CRRC (688009) with 70%+ market share. Safety-critical SIL4-level systems create extremely high switching barriers.

**Layer 4 — Braking Systems**: Disc brakes and regenerative braking — domestication rate exceeds 90%. Huawu (300095) is a representative independent supplier.

**Layer 5 — Bogies**: The most mechanically complex assembly, integrating axles, wheelsets, spring damping, brakes, and drive systems. Primarily developed and manufactured in-house by CRRC.

**Layer 6 — Body and Interior**: Aluminum alloy hollow-profile welded bodies, requiring extreme weld precision and pressure-tightness. Interior components involve many external contractors.

**Layer 7 — Track Materials**: Fasteners, rail, turnouts, catenary conductors. Jinyiyiye (601002) is the leading supplier of elastic rail fasteners for China's high-speed lines and for overseas HSR projects.

### 3. Industry's Three-Phase Technology Trajectory

Phase 1 (2004–2010): "Import-Digest-Absorb" — technology transfer agreements with Siemens, Bombardier, Alstom, and Kawasaki created the CRH Hexie series. Phase 2 (2011–2019): "Indigenous Innovation and Surpassing" — the Fuxing CR400 achieved fully proprietary IP and surpassed imported-generation benchmarks. Phase 3 (2020–present): "Self-Led Frontier" — CR450 development and mass-production of SiC traction systems mark China's transition from follower to leader on several technology fronts.

## Chapter II　Global Landscape: Five Blocs and China's Dominant Position

### 1. Global Rail Transit Equipment Market Overview

The global rail transit equipment market reached approximately USD 280–300 billion in 2025, spanning rolling stock (~~30%), signaling & control (~~15%), maintenance services (~~35%), and infrastructure (~~20%). China accounts for over one-third of the global market; Europe about one-quarter; North America around 10%; India, Southeast Asia, and Africa collectively around 20% and growing fastest.

### 2. The European Trio: Siemens, Alstom, Hitachi

**Siemens Mobility** reported exceptional FY2025 performance (year ending September 2025): Q3 revenue EUR 3.1 billion (+19% YoY); Q3 orders surged to EUR 7.9 billion (+240% YoY); full-year order backlog rose to EUR 52 billion (~3 years' revenue). FY2026 revenue growth guided at 8–10%. Key contracts include four HS2 UK high-speed rail contracts totaling USD 760 million. Siemens leads in signaling digitalization, with its ETCS platform deployed across dozens of countries.

**Alstom** — FY2025/26 data (year ending March 2026): 9-month order intake EUR 20 billion; 9-month sales EUR 13.9 billion; order backlog as of December 2025 exceeded EUR 100.3 billion, a record high; FY net profit (group share) EUR 324 million vs EUR 149 million the prior year, signaling that Bombardier integration headwinds have largely cleared.

**Hitachi Rail** completed the EUR 1.66 billion acquisition of Thales Ground Transportation Systems (GTS) in 2024, making it one of the world's largest rail signaling suppliers. Its product portfolio spans rolling stock (Azuma HSR in the UK), CBTC and ETCS signaling, and maintenance management systems.

### 3. East Asian Peers: Kawasaki and Hyundai Rotem

**Kawasaki Heavy Industries** focuses on Shinkansen rolling stock (N700/N700S) and has a track record in US metro markets. Under exchange-rate and cost pressure, its overseas competitive position has softened.

**Hyundai Rotem** is Korea's KTX supplier and participates in markets in the Middle East, Poland, and Australia. Its overall scale remains materially below that of the Chinese and European leaders.

### 4. CRRC: World's Largest, by a Wide Margin

CRRC (601766/1766.HK) generated CNY 273.1 billion (~USD 38 billion) in 2025 revenue — more than twice Siemens Mobility and 1.5 times Alstom. By rolling stock volume, CRRC accounts for approximately 40–45% of global market share.

CRRC's competitive advantages: (1) scale economies from a domestic market that generates unprecedented manufacturing volumes; (2) full-stack delivery capability — vehicles, signaling, maintenance, and financing as a single package; (3) policy-backed financing from CDB and Export-Import Bank of China, materially lowering the buyer's funding threshold.

### 5. Competitive Structure Summary

The global market is evolving toward a "China dominant, European trio strong, East Asian pair stable" six-pole structure. China leads on scale and cost; Europe leads on digital signaling and high-end system integration; Japan and Korea are solid domestically but globally constrained. India, Southeast Asia, and Africa represent the most important incremental battlegrounds for the next decade.

## Chapter III　PEST Analysis: Four Structural Drivers

### 1. Policy: Eight-Vertical-Eight-Horizontal Completion and Overseas Strategy Upgrade

The "Eight-Vertical-Eight-Horizontal" HSR network plan (published 2016, targeting ~45,000 km by 2035) has been effectively surpassed: operating mileage hit 50,000 km by end-2025. The main corridor construction phase is essentially complete; future investment focuses on densification, feeder lines, and quality upgrades rather than large-scale green-field corridor construction.

The 2025 National Railway Group completed network investment of approximately CNY 700 billion. Market-oriented reform has progressed since 2023, directing profitable lines toward market pricing and loss-making lines toward fiscal subsidy, while encouraging private capital participation in new projects.

High-speed rail overseas has been elevated to national strategic status within the Belt and Road framework. In 2025, the National Railway Group signed cooperation agreements with Spain, France, Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, and other countries at the UIC annual congress. CRRC's overseas new-order intake grew ~38% YoY, clearly establishing overseas orders as a primary growth driver.

### 2. Economics: Post-Construction Cycle and Aftermarket Rise

The economic logic of HSR construction underwent a structural shift in 2025. The peak investment cycle (2008–2019, driven by policy stimulus and regional development) added 3,000+ km/year at its height. From 2025 onward, with the trunk network essentially complete, annual new HSR additions have settled to 800–1,000 km. The 2026 plan includes approximately 2,000 km (including ongoing projects).

EMU maintenance follows a five-level mileage-based schedule, with Level-4 overhaul (~~1.2 million km) and Level-5 (~~1.8 million km) consuming the most labor, materials, and parts. The first large-scale Hexie CRH fleets, commissioned in 2007–2014, are entering their Level-4 and Level-5 maintenance windows during 2025–2030, with approximately 400 EMU sets per year requiring major overhaul. Aftermarket service revenue already exceeded CNY 40 billion in 2024 and is projected to grow at 15–20% CAGR through 2030.

On the overseas economics: China's HSR system consistently bids 30–50% below European and Japanese competitors, backed by concessional financing from policy banks. The Whoosh project (Indonesia), with total investment of approximately USD 11 billion largely supported by Chinese policy loans, exemplifies the integrated "finance-build-export" model that competitors struggle to replicate.

### 3. Society: Travel Pattern Shifts and Green Transition

Rail carried over 4 billion passengers in 2025, with HSR accounting for over 70%. As urbanization approaches 70%, travel demand is shifting from "rural-urban migration" to "metropolitan commuting and business travel." Per-capita carbon emissions from HSR are less than one-tenth of aviation's. Under China's "Dual Carbon" targets (carbon peak 2030, neutrality 2060), rail is explicitly prioritized as a green long-distance transport mode.

### 4. Technology: CR450 Leading, Hydrogen and Intelligence Entering the Frame

Three technology vectors: (1) Speed frontier — CR450's 453 km/h test record, lightweight design (50+ ton weight reduction vs. CR400), and SiC traction system, targeting 400 km/h commercial operation. (2) Green propulsion diversification — hydrogen fuel cell EMUs validated on test routes in Shandong and Hunan; energy-storage EMUs (supercapacitor + lithium) serving catenary-free sections. (3) Intelligent operation and digital twins — GOA4 fully autonomous driving deployed at scale on city metros; predictive maintenance platforms cutting servicing costs 10–20%.

## Chapter IV　China's Market Scale: The CNY 500 Billion-to-Trillion Roadmap

### 1. Scope Definition

Narrow scope: rolling stock (EMUs + locomotives) factory value only. Broad scope: rolling stock + components + signaling & control + maintenance + engineering machinery + track materials. This report adopts the broad scope for a complete economic picture.

### 2. 2025 Segment Estimates

Rolling stock: ~CNY 180 billion (HSR EMUs ~90 billion; urban rail ~60 billion; locomotives ~30 billion). Components: ~CNY 120 billion (traction systems ~35 billion; braking ~15 billion; bogies & precision parts ~20 billion; body aluminum ~15 billion; other electrical & interior ~35 billion). Signaling & control: ~CNY 40 billion (mainline signal ~25 billion; urban rail ~10 billion; intelligent O&M ~5 billion). Maintenance services: ~CNY 80 billion (EMU maintenance incl. overhauls ~45 billion; locomotive maintenance ~15 billion; line equipment ~20 billion). Engineering machinery & track materials: ~CNY 80 billion. **Aggregate: ~CNY 500 billion.**

### 3. CRRC's Market Share Profile

CRRC commands ~40–45% of the broad-scope market, but concentration varies dramatically by segment: HSR rolling stock >90%; urban rail >60%; traction systems (Times Electric, CRRC-controlled) >60%; railway signaling (CRRC, independent) >70%.

This hyper-concentrated structure is the institutional product of China's state-led construction model, enabling faster technology validation cycles than any other country.

### 4. Overseas + Aftermarket: Two New Growth Poles

China's 2025 broad-scope rail equipment export totaled approximately CNY 40–45 billion (8–9% of domestic market). By 2030, that share is projected to rise to 15–20%, with absolute value exceeding CNY 100 billion. The aftermarket segment, growing at 15–20% CAGR, is projected to surpass CNY 70 billion by 2028.

### 5. 2030 Market Forecast

Under base-case assumptions (annual new HSR 1,000–1,500 km; aftermarket peak release; overseas scale-up), the broad-scope market is forecast at CNY 600–650 billion by 2030, implying a 2026–2030 CAGR of ~4–5%. The structural significance: aftermarket rises from "negligible add-on service" to "pillar segment co-equal with rolling stock."

## Chapter V　Supply Chain Deep Dive: Seven Layers from Vehicles to Materials

### 1. Vehicle Manufacturing: CRRC's Six Core Factories

**CRRC Qingdao Sifang** — primary HSR production base; manufacturer of CR400AF/BF and the export Fuxing for Indonesia's Whoosh. Designed CRH380AL (486.1 km/h world record) and CR400 series; leads CR450 prototype development.

**CRRC Tangshan** — second major HSR production hub; first domesticated CRH3 (Siemens Velaro derivative) rolled off here. Leading aluminum body processing base.

**CRRC Changchun** — primary metro/light-rail manufacturer; export records spanning Brazil, Turkey, Israel, Ethiopia, Malaysia; highest internationalization rate among CRRC subsidiaries.

**CRRC Zhuzhou Electric Locomotive** — power-concentrated traction vehicles, maglev trains (Changsha Maglev Express, Beijing S1 Line); forms the tight "Zhuzhou traction system cluster" with Times Electric.

**CRRC Dalian** — diesel locomotives for freight and mining railways.

**CRRC Ziyang** — diesel locomotive exports to Africa, Southeast Asia, and the Middle East.

### 2. Traction Systems: Times Electric's SiC Breakthrough

Traction systems account for 20–25% of vehicle cost. CRRC Times Electric (688187) holds 60%+ domestic traction system share and is among the handful of global companies mass-producing railway-grade SiC power modules. Q1–Q3 2025 revenue CNY 18.8 billion (+14.9%); gross profit up over 36% YoY.

SiC vs. IGBT advantages: operating junction temperature >200°C; lower switching losses; lower conduction loss — enabling a ~30% volume reduction, ~25% weight reduction, and ~2 percentage point efficiency gain in traction converters.

### 3. Signaling: CRRC (688009)'s Deep Moat

CTCS (Chinese Train Control System) at Levels 3–4 underpins 300–350+ km/h operation, requiring SIL4 safety integrity (≤1 dangerous failure per 10 billion operating hours). CRRC commands 70%+ mainline signal market share. Entry barriers: 5–8 year R&D validation cycles, complex certification, and high on-site commissioning cost create near-insurmountable switching barriers.

### 4. Braking, Bogies, Aluminum Body, and Track Materials

Braking system domestic content rate exceeds 90%. Bogies (CRRC proprietary BOGIE series) fully meet domestic needs; high-precision wheels and bearings have some residual import dependency — a target area for domestic breakthrough. The CR450's weight-reduction program drives adoption of carbon fiber composites and higher-strength aluminum alloys. Jinyiyiye (601002) leads in HSR elastic fasteners, supplying Beijing-Shanghai, Beijing-Guangzhou, and overseas HSR projects including Whoosh and Hungary-Serbia.

## Chapter VI　Key Companies: Financials and Strategic Direction

### 1. CRRC (601766 / 1766.HK)

FY2025: Revenue CNY 273.1 billion (+10.8%); net profit CNY 13.2 billion (+6.4%). Rail equipment revenue CNY 123.6 billion (+11.9%); new industries revenue CNY 103.1 billion (+19.4%), already ~38% of total — a deliberate diversification strategy offsetting domestic construction slowdown. International revenue CNY 34.8 billion (+22.9%); international new orders ~CNY 65 billion (+38%), a record. Total new orders ~CNY 346.1 billion.

Key risks: ongoing compression of domestic new-line construction; National Railway Group debt constraining procurement pacing; retention of top engineers against private-sector competition; political and FX risk in overseas projects.

### 2. CRRC (688009 / 3969.HK)

FY2025: Revenue CNY 34.7 billion (+6.2%); net profit CNY 3.7 billion (+5.5%); net margin ~10.6%. Railway business CNY 21.4 billion (+13.7%); urban rail CNY 8.1 billion (-1.8%); overseas CNY 2.4 billion (-3.5%). Strategy: digital and intelligent signaling upgrade (cloud CTC, AI fault prediction), pivoting toward "intelligent rail operations service provider."

### 3. CRRC Times Electric (688187)

Q1–Q3 2025: Revenue CNY 18.8 billion (+14.9%); net profit ~CNY 2.7 billion (+11%); gross profit up >36% YoY. Dual growth logic: (1) rail traction system parts replacement from EMU major overhaul peak; (2) SiC power devices for EV and offshore wind as the second major business. CR450 mass production will require SiC converters at much higher unit value than conventional IGBT solutions.

### 4. Siwei Liekon / SWLK (603508)

FY2025: Revenue CNY 1.52 billion (+0.3%); net profit CNY 556 million (+1.4%). LKJ onboard control down 12%; HSR monitoring down 4%; locomotive security up 52%. Positioned as a beneficiary of aftermarket digitalization and intelligent diagnostics.

### 5. Huawu (300095)

FY2025: Revenue ~CNY 1.29 billion (+6.6%); rail braking system revenue >CNY 30 million (+130%); mining truck brake business simultaneously surged. Demonstrates fast growth in rail braking niche despite small absolute base.

### 6. Other Listed Companies

Jinyiyiye (601002) — HSR fastener leader with confirmed deliveries to overseas HSR projects. Kangni Mechanical & Electrical (603111) — urban rail door systems and platform screen doors. Yonggui Electric (300351) — rail electrical connectors. Zhonghe Technology (000925) — CBTC urban rail signaling independent supplier. Huihuang Technology (002296) — rail signaling and O&M equipment. CRRC Industry (600528) — rail turnouts and track engineering machinery.

### 7. International Competitors

Siemens Mobility: digital leadership, EUR 52 billion backlog, HS2 as largest single project; disadvantaged by cost in developing markets. Alstom: Bombardier integration essentially complete, EUR 100+ billion backlog (record), strong in India and Middle East. Hitachi Rail: full-stack vehicle + signaling capability post-Thales GTS acquisition; rolling stock concentrated in UK/Italy markets.

## Chapter VII　Industrial Clusters: The Ecosystem Ecology of Zhuzhou, Qingdao, Changchun, and Tangshan

### 1. Why Industrial Clusters Are the Key to Understanding the Industry

Rail transit equipment is heavy-asset, long-cycle, systems-integration manufacturing. The spatial distribution of the supply chain is highly concentrated, shaped by anchor vehicle factories attracting component suppliers into self-reinforcing clusters. China's rail equipment industrial geography is essentially a four-pole cluster map: Zhuzhou, Qingdao, Changchun, and Tangshan — plus specialized nodes at Dalian, Ziyang, and Chengdu.

Researchers seeking to understand the distribution of component suppliers within any given cluster can use **Tianxia Gongchang** ([www.tianxiagongchang.com](http://www.tianxiagongchang.com)), which indexes 4.8 million active factories searchable by region and industry category, making it particularly useful for supply chain due diligence and capacity verification.

### 2. Zhuzhou: China's "Power City"

Anchored by CRRC Zhuzhou Electric Locomotive (established 1936) and Times Electric, Zhuzhou has built China's most complete traction-system industrial ecosystem. The cluster's output exceeds CNY 150 billion annually, with 300+ component suppliers spanning traction, braking, electrical, and inspection equipment. Times Electric's Zhuzhou base vertically integrates from power chips and modules to complete traction converters, creating a near-replicable "co-evolved ecosystem" between rolling stock and traction systems.

### 3. Qingdao: The "Primary Factory" of HSR Rolling Stock

CRRC Qingdao Sifang is China's largest single HSR production base and primary HSR export site. CRH380AL, CR400, and CR450 prototype development all originated here. The Whoosh HSR Fuxing (Indonesian gauge/profile variant) was manufactured here, the most tangible proof of China's integrated HSR system export capability. The local cluster has 150+ component suppliers, with 60%+ local content rate. Qingdao's port access enables efficient aluminum structural import-export.

### 4. Changchun: Northern Base for Urban Rail and Export

CRRC Changchun (Changke) holds the broadest overseas export footprint among CRRC subsidiaries, with metro deliveries to Brazil (São Paulo), Turkey (Istanbul), Israel (Tel Aviv), Ethiopia (Addis Ababa), and Malaysia (Kuala Lumpur). It is China's most internationalised rolling stock factory for urban transit and a symbol of Northeast China's successful industrial transformation.

### 5. Tangshan: Northern HSR Rolling Stock Hub

CRRC Tangshan and Qingdao Sifang form the dual-core of China's HSR rolling stock production. Tangshan was where the first domesticated CRH3 (Siemens Velaro derivative) was produced. It is also a key aluminum car-body processing base. The local supply chain extends to elastic fasteners (Jinyiyiye) and other track materials, giving the cluster multi-layer depth.

### 6. Dalian, Ziyang, and Chengdu: Specialized Nodes

CRRC Dalian focuses on diesel locomotives for freight and mining. CRRC Ziyang is the primary diesel locomotive export base for Africa and Southeast Asia — one of China's key "one-port" export facilities. Chengdu's rapid metro expansion (500+ km in operation) has seeded a Southwest urban-rail equipment cluster in its own right.

## Chapter VIII　Segment Deep Dives: CR400 System, Inter-city Expansion, Overseas Footprint, and Aftermarket Rise

### 1. CR400 Series: Mature Production, Deepening Technology

The Fuxing CR400 series, operating at 350 km/h commercially, is the world's highest commercial-speed HSR fleet in mass operation. CR400AF (8-car, ~1,083 passengers) and CR400BF (16-car, 2,000+ passengers), extendable to a 17-car super-formation, are the highest single-train capacity HSR vehicles globally. Versus the CRH series: interior noise <65 dB; energy consumption ~17% lower than CRH380; modular design reduces maintenance complexity.

### 2. CR450: Prelude to the 400 km/h Era

Design speed: 450 km/h. Target commercial speed: 400 km/h. Test record: 453 km/h (Beijing-Shanghai HSR, 2025). Weight reduction: 50+ tons vs. CR400 via carbon fiber composites and advanced aluminum alloys. Traction: new-generation SiC traction converter from Times Electric. Status: ~300,000 km completed as of February 2026; full 600,000 km validation expected by end-2026; design finalization and mass production entry projected 2027. CR450 is the only EMU in the world currently targeting 400 km/h commercial operation.

### 3. Inter-city Rail and Suburban Rail: The Metropolitan Battleground

With urbanization shifting from single-city expansion to metropolitan-area integration, inter-city rail (5,000+ km in operation, covering Yangtze River Delta, Pearl River Delta, Jing-Jin-Ji) and suburban rail (120–160 km/h) are the fastest-growing sub-segments. Representative projects: Shanghai Metro Regional Rail (Jiamin Line, Chongming Line), Beijing Suburban Railway (Sub-center Line, S11), Guangzhou Metro Express.

### 4. Overseas: Four Flagship System-Export Projects

**Whoosh (Indonesia)**: 143 km, 350 km/h, opened October 2023, 13 million+ passengers by end-2025. Complete system export: CRRC rolling stock + CRRC signaling + CRRC construction EPC.

**Laos-China Railway**: 1,000 km, opened December 2021; 2025 freight volume +15% YoY, passengers +~2% YoY. The most commercially successful BRI rail project, validating Chinese system reliability in tropical climates and complex terrain.

**Hungary-Serbia Railway**: Serbia section fully open; Hungary section under construction. Historic breakthrough into EU-member nations.

**China-Thailand HSR**: Phase 2 government-approved; linking with Laos-China Railway will create a Bangkok-to-Chengdu rail corridor — one of the BRI's most strategically important infrastructure projects.

Also: China-Kyrgyzstan-Uzbekistan Railway entered preliminary construction tendering; CRRC expanding equipment supply in Saudi Arabia and Africa.

### 5. Aftermarket Maintenance: The Second Structural Growth Engine

EMU maintenance runs from Level-1 (15,000 km checks) through Level-5 (1.8 million km, comprehensive overhaul). Level-5 cost is ~20–25% of a new vehicle. The 2007–2014 CRH fleet cohort enters Level-4 and Level-5 windows in 2025–2030, with ~400 sets/year requiring major overhaul. Level-5 alone represents ~CNY 12–15 billion annually; combined with Levels 3–4 and routine parts, the total aftermarket exceeds CNY 40 billion/year and is growing rapidly. Core beneficiaries: CRRC (original-equipment overhaul) and Times Electric (traction system parts replacement), plus independent component suppliers of braking parts, interior materials, and electrical components.

## Chapter IX　Technology Evolution: Speed Limits, Green Propulsion, and the Digital Future

### 1. CR450 and the Engineering Challenges of 400 km/h Commercial Operation

At 400 km/h, four engineering dimensions are far more demanding than at 350 km/h:

**Wheel-rail interaction**: Dynamic wheel-rail forces scale with velocity squared. CR450 requires higher-hardness wheel steel, tighter rail surface micro-geometry, and more frequent inspection cycles.

**Pantograph-catenary**: Pantograph dewirement rate (contact wire loss frequency) escalates sharply at high speed. CR450 addresses this through aerodynamic pantograph shaping and catenary pre-tensioning optimization.

**Aerodynamic effects**: Tunnel piston effects at 400 km/h require enlarged tunnel clearances or aerodynamic buffer structures at portals.

**Signaling and control**: At 400 km/h, a train travels 111+ meters per second — the CTCS-4 system must provide adequate braking distance calculation and emergency response in an extremely narrow time window.

### 2. Green Propulsion: Hydrogen and Energy-Storage EMUs

**Hydrogen fuel cell EMUs**: Zero-emission operation (water vapor exhaust only). CRRC Qingdao Sifang's green hydrogen EMU validated on test routes in Shandong and Hunan, achieving ~600 km range per refuel. Key constraints: hydrogen storage density, sparse refueling infrastructure, and fuel cell stack durability. Most likely 2030-era application: short-distance inter-city or tourist routes on non-electrified sections.

**Energy-storage EMUs**: Supercapacitor/lithium storage captures regenerative braking energy for use on catenary-free sections. Much lower cost than hydrogen; already commercially deployed on multiple tram lines. Near-term practical option for "last 100 km" non-electrified extensions.

### 3. Intelligent Operation and Digital Twins

**GOA4 autonomous operation**: Standard on new Chinese urban metro lines (Beijing, Shanghai, Guangzhou, Shenzhen), achieving 30–90 second headways. On the HSR side, energy-optimization algorithms reduce traction consumption by 5–8% while maintaining schedules.

**Digital twins**: Real-time acquisition of vibration, temperature, and electrical parameters from wheelsets, bogies, traction, and braking systems builds a digital mirror of each EMU. This enables transition from "planned maintenance" (mileage-triggered) to "predictive maintenance" (condition-triggered), cutting maintenance costs 10–20%.

### 4. SiC Power Semiconductors: Traction System Material Revolution

SiC vs. IGBT: higher operating temperature (>200°C junction), lower switching and conduction losses — resulting in ~30% smaller converter volume, ~25% lighter weight, ~2 percentage point efficiency gain. Times Electric is the only Chinese company mass-producing railway-grade SiC modules; its first-mover advantage is unlikely to be displaced before CR450 mass production (2027–2030). Domestic SiC substrate cost reduction (6-inch to 8-inch wafer domestication) will progressively improve the value proposition of SiC converters.

## Chapter X　Risks and Challenges: Five Structural Pressures

### 1. Domestic New-Line Contraction: Phase-Weak Rolling Stock Demand

Peak HSR new-line: ~3,500 km/year in 2019. Current: ~800–1,000 km/year in 2025, a >70% decline. If annual new HSR stabilizes at 1,000–1,500 km, rolling stock procurement will stabilize at 30–40% below peak, creating sustained top-line pressure on CRRC's vehicle manufacturing segment. Buffers: stable urban rail demand; surging overseas orders; CRH fleet retirement replacements; CR450 creating a new procurement wave.

### 2. Fiscal and Debt Constraints: Dual Pressure from National Railways and Local Governments

National Railway Group's cumulative HSR construction debt is estimated at 6–7 trillion yuan, with annual interest burden in the hundreds of billions. Revenue growth from HSR operations barely offsets rising interest, constraining procurement budgets. Local-government-funded inter-city and suburban rail projects face fiscal headwinds from the contraction in land sales revenue, with some projects experiencing construction delays.

### 3. Overseas Political Risk and Localization Pressure

Malaysia's Kuala Lumpur-Singapore HSR has been deferred multiple times through government changes. Several African projects have encountered delays from loan-term disputes. Tightening "local content" requirements in host countries challenge cost advantages and require deeper in-country operational presence.

### 4. Technology Sanctions and Export Controls

High-end power semiconductors (IGBT/SiC wafers), precision metrology equipment, and advanced controllers have residual import dependencies. Escalating export controls raise supply chain risk. European countries have introduced additional security requirements for Chinese suppliers in public rail procurement — a permanent entry barrier for the European market.

### 5. International Competition and Standards Conflict

Siemens and Alstom are deepening emerging-market investments and local partnerships. The slow progress of TSI/EN and GB/T/TB mutual recognition creates significant adaptation certification costs for Chinese HSR entering European-standard markets. India's Bullet Train project (Shinkansen technology), Southeast Asian rail upgrades, and Middle East network expansion will be the key competitive battlegrounds for the next decade.

## Chapter XI　2026–2030 Forecast: New Coordinates for an Industry in Engine Transition

### 1. Market Size Scenarios

**Base case** (new HSR 1,000–1,500 km/year; aftermarket peak release; overseas ~20% CAGR): 2027 broad-scope ~CNY 550 billion; 2030 ~CNY 600–650 billion; 2026–2030 CAGR ~4–5%.

**Optimistic case** (overseas >30% CAGR, early aftermarket peak): 2030 ~CNY 700–750 billion; CAGR ~7–9%.

**Pessimistic case** (<800 km/year domestic; major overseas projects deferred): 2030 ~CNY 550 billion; CAGR ~1–2%.

### 2. Four Structural Predictions

**Aftermarket overtakes domestic rolling stock: estimated 2027–2028.** Maintenance (~CNY 80 billion in 2025, growing at 15–20% CAGR) overtakes domestic rolling stock (compressed to ~CNY 120 billion by new-line contraction) as the largest single domestic segment — the structural milestone of the industry's manufacturing-to-service transition.

**Exports rise to 15–20% of broad-scope market.** From ~CNY 40–45 billion today to ~CNY 90–120 billion by 2030. Southeast Asia, South Asia, Middle East, and Africa are the primary increment markets; Europe limited but strategically significant.

**CR450 commercial entry: 2027–2029.** After validation finalization, commercial launch most likely on a high-density trunk line (e.g., Beijing-Shanghai or Chengdu-Chongqing central corridor). Mass production triggers SiC traction, new braking, and lightweight materials technology-upgrade procurement across the supply chain.

**Green technology crossing the commercial threshold.** Hydrogen EMUs transition from test-line validation to small-batch demonstration runs; SiC traction achieves larger-scale penetration; GOA4 autonomous operation becomes the standard for new urban metro lines.

### 3. Supply Chain Displacement and Competition Bifurcation

The current concentration in CRRC and CRRC (signaling) will partially loosen in the aftermarket: standardized component replacement (braking parts, interior materials, electrical components) is relatively open to independent suppliers. The competitive bifurcation will accelerate: strong players (CRRC, CRRC, Times Electric) capture overseas and aftermarket primary shares; mid-tier suppliers (Jinyiyiye, Kangni, Yonggui) grow with subsegment recoveries; commodity suppliers without technology differentiation face structural pressure.

## Chapter XII　Conclusion: Speed Is Set — the Engine Is Changing

China's first thirty years of high-speed rail is a history with speed as its axis: from 48 km/h average to 350 km/h, from zero HSR mileage to 50,000 km, from technology importer to technology exporter. Each of these three transformations is an independent industrial miracle. By 2026, this history has turned past its "construction peak" chapter and entered a new cycle of fundamentally different incremental logic.

**First, the domestic battleground has shifted from "new construction" to "existing network."** The 50,000 km HSR estate means the marginal value of each additional kilometer of new line is declining, while the maintenance and upgrade value of existing assets is rising. The Level-5 overhaul peak, digital O&M upgrades, and line facility renovations — these "invisible infrastructure" investments will generate enormous industrial value over the next five to ten years.

**Second, the incremental engine has shifted from "domestic" to "overseas."** CRRC's 2025 international new orders of CNY 65 billion (+38% YoY) are the clearest signal yet. Whoosh's successful operation, the Laos-China Railway's freight growth, Hungary-Serbia's extension — all validate the exportability of the Chinese HSR system: not just "the train," but the complete "build-operate-finance" solution that developing countries urgently need. **Tianxia Gongchang** ([www.tianxiagongchang.com](http://www.tianxiagongchang.com)), with data on 4.8 million active manufacturing factories across China including rail component producers, provides overseas project teams with a tool to rapidly audit domestic supply-chain capacity during competitive bidding.

**Third, technology leadership has shifted from "catching up" to "blazing the frontier."** CR450's 453 km/h record and the mass production of SiC traction systems position China at the international frontier of rail technology. This is not "we can do it too" — it is a declaration that China is now defining what the next generation of high-speed rail looks like.

**Fourth, industry value is shifting from "manufacturing-dominated" to "manufacturing plus services."** The rise of the aftermarket is the natural maturation of the industry: a 50,000 km HSR network and 4,500+ EMU sets in operation create a maintenance market worth hundreds of billions annually — still in its early growth stage.

China's rail transit equipment industry's fundamentals are robust: technology leadership, complete supply chain, clear cost advantages, and overseas window open. The only task remaining is to find operating approaches matched to the new growth logic of the "post-construction-peak" reality. That differentiation has begun, and will accelerate through 2026–2030.

**Main Topic:** This report from 天下工厂产业研究院 (Tianxia Gongchang Industry Research Institute) systematically examines China's high-speed rail EMU and rail transit equipment industry as of 2026, covering market structure, supply chain, key company financials, technology frontiers, and development outlook.

**Key Findings:**
- **Market Size:** China's rail transit equipment market reached ~CNY 500 billion in 2025 (broad basis: rolling stock ~180B, components ~120B, signaling ~40B, maintenance ~80B, engineering ~80B). Forecast to exceed CNY 650 billion by 2030.
- **Historical Context:** China went from 48 km/h average train speed (1993) and zero HSR to 50,000 km of HSR by December 2025 — exceeding the rest of the world combined. The country now commands ~70% of global high-speed rail mileage.
- **Competitive Landscape:** CRRC (601766) dominates with CNY 273.1 billion revenue in 2025 (+10.8%), ~40-45% global rolling stock share. CRRC (688009) monopolizes railway signaling (>70% share). CRRC Times Electric (688187) leads traction systems (>60% share). The supply chain is hyper-concentrated with domestic substitution essentially complete.
- **Growth Engines:** (1) Overseas orders surging — CRRC's international new orders hit ~CNY 65 billion in 2025 (+38% YoY). Key projects: Whoosh Indonesia (13M+ passengers), Laos-China Railway, Hungary-Serbia, China-Thailand HSR. (2) Aftermarket maintenance entering peak cycle — ~400 EMU sets/year requiring Level-5 overhaul through 2025-2030, with aftermarket revenue exceeding CNY 40 billion and growing at 15-20% CAGR.
- **Technology Frontier:** CR450 completed 453 km/h test (global record), targeting 400 km/h commercial operation post-2027. SiC traction systems, hydrogen fuel cell EMUs, and GOA4 autonomous operation are all advancing.
- **Risks:** Domestic new-line contraction (from 3,500 km/yr peak to 800-1,000 km/yr); National Railway Group's 6-7 trillion yuan debt burden; overseas political risk; export controls on semiconductors; international standards conflicts.

**Supply Chain (7 Layers):** Vehicle integration (CRRC subsidiaries), traction systems (Times Electric), signaling (CRRC), braking systems (domestic >90%), bogies (CRRC proprietary), body/interior, track materials (Jinyiyiye). Four main industrial clusters: Zhuzhou (power systems), Qingdao (primary HSR production), Changchun (urban rail/exports), Tangshan (northern HSR hub).

**Forecast (Base Case 2026-2030):** Broad-scope market CAGR ~4-5% to CNY 600-650 billion. Aftermarket expected to overtake domestic rolling stock as largest segment by 2027-2028. Exports projected to rise to 15-20% of market (CNY 90-120 billion) by 2030.

**Conclusion:** The industry has passed its 'construction peak' and entered a new cycle where the battleground shifts from new construction to existing network maintenance, from domestic to overseas markets, from catching up to frontier-blazing, and from manufacturing-dominated to manufacturing-plus-services.

# China: Latest wave of openings brings faster and more automated metros

By Railway Gazette |

The number of fully automated metro lines in China is increasing rapidly as cities seek to accommodate urban growth by improving efficiency and increasing capacity through higher frequencies. **Toma Bačić** reviews the latest tranche of openings.

As has become traditional, the closing weeks of 2025 saw a raft of metro projects inaugurated across China, including several new routes as well as extensions to existing lines. Notable trends to be seen in the latest round of openings have been an increase in design speeds, as cities continue to expand and lines get longer, and greater use of GoA4 fully automatic train operation permitting more frequent services to be worked at shorter headways.

### Dongguan joins the club

November 28 saw the inauguration of the [first metro line in Dongguan](https://www.railwaygazette.com/data/guangzhou-foshan-and-dongguan-region-map-of-pearl-river-delta/54055.article), a new city in the middle of the Guangdong – [Hong Kong](https://www.railwaygazette.com/data/hong-kong-city-map/54058.article) – Macao Greater Bay Area, east of [Guangzhou](https://www.railwaygazette.com/maps-and-data/guangzhou-foshan-and-dongguan-city-map/54055.article) and north of Shenzhen. This megalopolis consisting of nine cities and two special administrative regions is now the largest and most inhabited urban area in the world, with a total population of approximately 86 million people.

![L1_Train_(PM246_01x005-006)_entering_Houde_Station,_Dongguan_Rail_Transit_20251228 (image Tim Wu Wikipedia)](https://www.railwaygazette.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/02/77396_l1_train_pm246_01x005006_entering_houde_station_dongguan_rail_transit_20251228imagetimwuwikipedia_659825.jpg)

The first metro line in Dongguan opened on November 28. The driverless route has an operating speed of 120 km/h.

Dongguan metro Line 1 has been built for 120 km/h running and equipped for GoA4 driverless operation. The 57·5 km line links Dongguan Xi station in the west to Meitang in the southeast, with 49·4 km of the route in tunnel. It is worked by a fleet of 34 six-car Type B trainsets, which were ordered from [CRRC](https://www.railwaygazette.com/crrc/2062.subject) Puzhen in 2022; the first train was delivered to Daojiao depot in December 2024.

A planned second phase will see Line 1 extended to Huangpu New Port, where interchange will be provided with Guangzhou metro Line 5. A southeastern extension would run to SUAT (Shenzhen Polytechnic University), where it will connect to a branch of Shenzhen Line 6.

Several more extensions are envisaged in the Dongguan metro development plans for 2022-30 and 2030-35, providing additional links to both Guangzhou and Shenzhen.
