# Dynamic headway control for capacity optimization: a critical review

Zhanibek Shukamanov 1\*

Gulfariza Suleimenova 2

1. Department of Automation and Telecommunications, M.Kh. Dulaty Taraz University, Taraz, Kazakhstan

2. Department of Automation and Control, ALT M. Tynyshpayev University, Almaty, Kazakhstan

Article metrics

## Abstract

Increasing traffic density and the deployment of digital signalling technologies are transforming railway capacity from a static infrastructure constraint into a real-time controllable system-performance variable. This critical review provides a system-level analysis of dynamic headway control and its impact on effective railway capacity within closed-loop operational environments. Modelling paradigms, including analytical methods, microscopic simulation, optimisation-based traffic management, and artificial intelligence approaches, are comparatively assessed with respect to control capability, scalability, real-time applicability, and sensitivity to disturbances. The review shows that conventional planning-oriented capacity assessment systematically overestimates achievable throughput because it neglects traffic stability, disturbance propagation, and feedback-based regulation. The evolution of control architectures from fixed-block signalling to moving-block systems, predictive traffic management, and virtual coupling is interpreted as a transition from infrastructure-limited to control-limited capacity. A unified conceptual framework is proposed that links control architecture, headway dynamics, traffic stability, and effective capacity within a cyber-physical control loop. This perspective enables the identification of key research gaps, including the lack of integrated real-time models and the limited incorporation of artificial intelligence into safety-critical control. Future intelligent railway operation is expected to be based on digital twins, reinforcement learning, and distributed coordination, enabling continuous capacity regulation under stochastic conditions.

## 1 Introduction

The continuous growth of passenger and freight transportation demand has turned railway capacity into a key performance indicator of modern transport systems and a central challenge for infrastructure managers and operators. Unlike other transport modes, the expansion of railway capacity through the construction of new lines is associated with high investment costs, long implementation periods, and significant environmental constraints. Consequently, increasing the throughput of existing infrastructure by improving operational control and signalling technologies has become a priority research direction. In this context, train headway is the temporal or spatial separation between consecutive trains is widely recognised as one of the dominant factors limiting line capacity and operational efficiency (He et al., 2022).

Traditionally, railway traffic has been governed by fixed-block signalling principles, where the infrastructure is divided into discrete track sections and safe train separation is ensured by conservative braking distance assumptions. In this context, fixed-block signalling refers to a system in which the railway line is divided into discrete track sections, and a train is allowed to enter a section only if it is completely unoccupied, resulting in conservative and spatially rigid separation rules. Moving-block signalling removes this discretisation by continuously calculating a safe braking distance based on real-time train position, speed, and performance characteristics, allowing trains to operate with dynamically updated separation. Such concepts are implemented in modern communication-based train control (CBTC) systems and are partially reflected in advanced European Train Control System (ETCS Level 3) and Chinese Train Control System (CTCS-3) architectures. Virtual coupling represents a further evolution of moving-block principles, in which trains operate in a coordinated manner based on relative motion and train-to-train communication, effectively forming dynamically controlled platoons with reduced separation while maintaining safety through cooperative control strategies.

Although such systems provide a high level of safety and operational robustness, they inherently impose static headway margins that lead to underutilisation of infrastructure capacity (Spunei et al., 2014). The transition toward moving-block and communication-based train control (CBTC) systems has introduced the possibility of continuously updated movement authority and dynamically calculated train separation, enabling a substantial reduction in operational headways and a corresponding increase in traffic density (Felez and Vaquero-Serrano, 2023). Recent studies demonstrate that dynamic headway models based on real-time trajectory prediction and iterative control strategies can significantly decrease train spacing while maintaining safety constraints, thus improving network throughput and service reliability (He et al., 2022; Usama and Koutsopoulos, 2025).

Despite these technological advances, the relationship between headway control and railway capacity remains insufficiently understood from a system-level perspective. One of the fundamental problems is the lack of a unified and universally accepted definition of railway capacity. In this study, this limitation is addressed by adopting a control-oriented perspective on capacity, in which different modelling approaches are compared not only in terms of absolute throughput values but also with respect to their underlying assumptions, ability to represent real-time control, and sensitivity to disturbances. Rather than relying on a single definition, the analysis focuses on relative performance, scalability, and robustness across modelling frameworks, allowing a consistent comparison despite the absence of a universally accepted capacity metric. Existing approaches distinguish between theoretical capacity, representing idealised maximum throughput under deterministic conditions, and operational (or effective) capacity, which accounts for real-world constraints such as traffic heterogeneity, timetable structure, and disturbance propagation. In this paper, the terms *operational capacity* and *effective capacity* are used interchangeably to describe achievable performance under realistic operating conditions, while the term *practical capacity* is not treated as a separate category in order to avoid ambiguity. However, most capacity assessment methodologies are still based on static or quasi-static formulations, where system conditions are assumed to change slowly and control decisions are based on aggregated or time-averaged parameters rather than continuous real-time updates, do not adequately account for real-time control actions, stochastic delays, or dynamic interactions between trains (Ramdas and Chapman, 2017). As a result, conventional capacity metrics often overestimate achievable performance and fail to capture the stability of traffic flow under disturbed conditions.

Another limitation of the current research landscape is that existing modelling approaches, although diverse and well-developed, do not capture the full system-level dynamics of railway operations. Analytical formulations, traffic-flow models, discrete-event simulations, and optimisation-based methods are frequently developed in isolation and applied to specific operational scenarios. For instance, simulation studies incorporating stochastic dispatching delays have shown that the consideration of operational variability leads to more realistic capacity estimates, particularly in partially automated railway systems (Shukamanov et al., 2025). However, these models are rarely integrated with control-oriented formulations capable of describing adaptive headway regulation in real time. Similarly, emerging intelligent control techniques, including predictive control, machine-learning-based trajectory estimation, and cooperative train control, are typically evaluated in terms of local performance indicators rather than system-wide capacity effects.

From a control-systems perspective, headway should not be treated merely as a safety constraint but as a dynamic and controllable variable that directly determines traffic flow stability, energy efficiency, and infrastructure utilisation. Real-time regulation of train motion and dwell times has already been shown to reduce headway variance and stabilise metro operations through feedback control mechanisms formulated as stochastic optimal control problems (Schanzenbacher et al., 2018). Moreover, recent research on virtual coupling and cooperative train operation demonstrates the potential for distributed and consensus-based control architectures to further minimise train separation and enable flexible, high-density traffic management (Wu et al., 2023). These developments indicate a paradigm shift from infrastructure-based capacity enhancement to control-driven performance optimisation.

However, the practical realisation of dynamic headway control faces several unresolved challenges. Communication latency, positioning uncertainty, safety certification requirements, and the trade-off between robustness and maximum throughput limit the achievable capacity gains in real networks. Even in moving-block systems, theoretical reductions in train separation are often constrained by station dwell times, mixed traffic operations, and the need for operational buffers (Versluis et al., 2024). Therefore, a critical reassessment of existing modelling paradigms and control architectures is required in order to identify the actual performance limits and research gaps.

In light of these considerations, this paper provides a critical review of dynamic headway control as a system-level mechanism for capacity optimisation. Unlike conventional railway-oriented surveys, the study adopts a control- and performance-driven perspective that links headway regulation, traffic dynamics, and infrastructure utilisation within a unified analytical framework. The review systematically compares modelling approaches in terms of their ability to represent real-time control, scalability, and sensitivity to disturbances, and analyses the effectiveness of modern control architectures for increasing network throughput. Based on this analysis, key limitations of current methodologies are identified and future research directions toward intelligent, adaptive, and distributed railway traffic control are outlined.

## 2 Methodology

This study adopts a control-oriented analytical review methodology to investigate the role of dynamic headway control in railway capacity optimization. While the review does not strictly follow a formal systematic review protocol (e.g., PRISMA), it applies a structured and transparent literature selection and analysis process.

The literature selection focused on peer-reviewed journal articles and recent conference proceedings published primarily within the last 10–15 years, with emphasis on studies addressing railway signalling systems, headway control, traffic-flow modelling, and real-time control architectures. Key databases and sources included Scopus-indexed journals and major transportation and control-systems venues. Priority was given to works that explicitly analyse real-time control mechanisms, system-level performance, and scalability aspects.

The review is guided by the following research questions:

How do existing modelling approaches represent train headway under real-time operational conditions?

To what extent do current control frameworks capture disturbance propagation and traffic stability at the network level?

What are the limitations of existing approaches in terms of scalability, robustness, and integration with modern signalling systems?

Different modelling paradigms, including analytical formulations, traffic-flow models, simulation-based approaches, and optimization-based control methods, were comparatively analysed in terms of their ability to represent real-time headway regulation, disturbance propagation, and system scalability. Particular attention was given to modern control architectures such as moving-block systems, predictive control, and cooperative train operation.

The comparative synthesis of these approaches enabled the identification of key methodological limitations and the formulation of a system-level framework linking headway control, traffic stability, and infrastructure utilisation.

## 3 Dynamic headway as a control variable

### 3.1 From static safety margins to dynamic control

In this study, the term *dynamic headway control* is used to denote the general framework in which train separation is continuously updated based on real-time information, trajectory prediction, and system state. *Adaptive headway control* is considered a specific implementation within this framework, in which control parameters such as speed, dwell time, and braking profiles are actively adjusted through feedback mechanisms to maintain system stability and optimise performance under varying operational conditions.

The traditional determination of train separation has historically been rooted in the concept of fixed safety envelopes derived from worst-case braking scenarios and predefined signalling logic. In these approaches, the minimum permissible headway is calculated using conservative assumptions regarding train deceleration, driver reaction, track conditions, and communication delays. While such formulations guarantee fail-safe operation, they implicitly transform headway into a static constraint rather than a controllable system variable. As a consequence, infrastructure utilisation is limited not by the physical performance of rolling stock or real traffic conditions, but by predefined safety buffers that remain unchanged during operation. This paradigm is still embedded in many capacity assessment methodologies and dispatching practices, particularly in networks operating with legacy signalling or semi-automatic block systems (Versluis et al., 2024).

A fundamental limitation of static headway modelling lies in the use of fixed braking distance assumptions. In this context, braking distance refers to a scalar estimate of the minimum safe separation required to prevent collision under predefined conditions, whereas the braking curve represents the dynamic deceleration profile of a train as a function of speed, distance, or time. Static formulations typically approximate safety constraints using simplified or deterministic braking curves for both leading and following trains, thereby reducing the problem to fixed separation distances. Such representations neglect variations in adhesion, train mass, traction control strategies, and real-time speed profiles, which influence the actual braking behaviour under operational conditions. As shown in recent modelling studies, braking distance is frequently treated as a constant parameter, while longitudinal train dynamics, gradients, and energy-efficient driving modes are neglected, leading to an overestimation of the required separation distance (Sofroniou, 2021). This simplification introduces structural rigidity into the control process and prevents the system from exploiting the actual performance envelope of modern rolling stock. In high-density operations, such conservative assumptions translate directly into reduced throughput and increased sensitivity to perturbations, since recovery margins must also be embedded in the timetable.

The transition toward moving-block and communication-based train control systems has challenged this static safety paradigm by enabling continuous train positioning and real-time exchange of motion authority. In these architectures, headway is no longer determined by the occupancy of discrete track sections but by the dynamically computed safe braking distance relative to the preceding train. However, even in advanced implementations, many operational models still rely on quasi-static formulations in which the separation distance is updated periodically but not optimised as a function of predicted train trajectories (Basile et al., 2019). This reveals a conceptual gap between the technological capability of modern signalling systems and the control strategies used to manage traffic flow.

Recent research demonstrates that the incorporation of trajectory prediction into headway computation fundamentally changes the nature of train separation control (He et al., 2022; Kunimatsu et al., 2019). Hybrid approaches combining model-based estimation with machine-learning techniques allow the future motion of the leading train to be forecast within the braking horizon of the following train. This enables iterative control algorithms to continuously adapt the separation distance to actual operating conditions rather than worst-case scenarios. Simulation results for communication-based train control environments indicate that such dynamic headway formulations can reduce inter-train distance by more than 60% while maintaining safety constraints, thereby significantly increasing traffic density without infrastructure expansion (Usama and Koutsopoulos, 2025).

These results are not contradictory but reflect different modelling assumptions. The reported reduction in inter-train distance represents a theoretical potential achieved under controlled conditions, where accurate trajectory prediction and coordinated control allow the system to operate close to safety limits. In contrast, the observed capacity overestimation arises from stochastic operational effects such as dwell-time variability, heterogeneous rolling stock, and disturbance propagation, which are not fully captured in deterministic formulations. Consequently, while dynamic headway control can significantly reduce nominal train separation, the effective capacity gain in real railway systems is moderated by variability and stability constraints. This highlights the importance of integrating stochastic dynamics and disturbance sensitivity into control-oriented headway models.

Despite these advances, the shift from static safety margins to dynamic control is far from complete. One of the key unresolved issues is the limited integration of stochastic operational effects into headway models. Real railway traffic is characterised by dwell-time variability, heterogeneous rolling stock, temporary speed restrictions, and dispatching interventions. When these factors are ignored, capacity calculations based on deterministic headway values systematically overestimate achievable throughput. Discrete-event simulation studies that explicitly incorporate random delays have shown that neglecting stochastic variability can lead to capacity overestimations of up to 30%, highlighting the need for adaptive control strategies capable of responding to real-time disturbances (Shukamanov et al., 2025).

Another critical aspect concerns the control architecture required to support dynamic headway regulation. Static formulations assume a unidirectional safety logic in which the following train passively reacts to the behaviour of the leader. In contrast, dynamic control frameworks treat train motion as a coupled system in which speed commands, braking profiles, and dwell times are coordinated through continuous feedback. This shift transforms headway from a geometric spacing parameter into an emergent property of the traffic flow dynamics. Such a perspective is consistent with system-level traffic management approaches, where capacity is determined not only by minimum separation but also by the stability of train sequences under varying demand and disturbance conditions (Pachl, 2022).

However, the implementation of fully adaptive headway control introduces new trade-offs between performance, robustness, and computational complexity. Real-time optimisation requires reliable communication, high-precision positioning, and fast decision-making algorithms. In the presence of communication latency or temporary data loss, the control system must revert to more conservative separation rules, effectively reintroducing static safety margins. This hybrid operational mode remains insufficiently explored in the literature and represents a major barrier to the practical deployment of dynamic headway strategies in mixed-traffic and long-distance railway networks.

From a capacity perspective, the persistence of static modelling assumptions reflects a deeper methodological issue: the separation between safety verification and performance optimisation. In conventional approaches, safety constraints are imposed *a priori* and capacity is evaluated within these limits. In dynamic control frameworks, safety and performance become interdependent variables that must be managed simultaneously through predictive and feedback control. The absence of integrated models capable of capturing this interaction explains why many existing studies report theoretical headway reductions that cannot be realised in real operation.

In summary, the evolution from fixed safety margins to dynamic headway control represents a transition from infrastructure-based to control-driven capacity enhancement. Static braking assumptions, deterministic separation rules, and the lack of adaptation to stochastic traffic conditions remain the primary factors limiting infrastructure utilisation. Although modern signalling technologies provide the data and communication capabilities required for real-time control, the modelling paradigms used for capacity assessment are still largely based on conservative and decoupled formulations. Bridging this gap requires the development of control-oriented headway models that integrate trajectory prediction, disturbance propagation, and system stability into a unified framework.

### 3.2 Control parameters shaping headway dynamics

In a dynamic traffic management environment, train separation is no longer determined solely by infrastructure constraints but emerges from the interaction of multiple controllable variables that govern the longitudinal motion of trains and the temporal structure of operations. From a control-systems perspective, headway becomes a state-dependent output influenced by speed regulation, braking behaviour, dwell time management, communication latency, and inter-train coupling mechanisms. Understanding how these parameters shape headway dynamics is essential for transitioning from static safety envelopes to performance-oriented railway control.

Speed constitutes the primary control input in real-time headway regulation. Modern automatic train operation systems continuously adjust traction commands in order to maintain stability of train sequences and prevent the amplification of disturbances. Unlike timetable-based regulation, where speed profiles are predefined, model-based control allows the velocity of each train to be modified as a function of the predicted motion of neighbouring trains and downstream constraints. Recent optimal control formulations demonstrate that speed modulation can be used to reshape headway without invoking full braking cycles, thereby reducing energy consumption while preserving throughput. In dense metro operations, feedback-based speed harmonisation has been shown to decrease headway variance and improve service regularity by actively damping traffic waves (Polinder et al., 2021).

Closely related to speed control is the treatment of braking curves as adjustable rather than invariant safety functions. In classical signalling logic, braking distance is derived from worst-case deceleration and remains fixed throughout operation. In contrast, dynamic control frameworks treat the braking profile as a function of real-time adhesion estimates, train mass, and control system response time. Moving-block implementations with continuous supervision enable the computation of a moving safe-braking envelope that evolves with the instantaneous state of the train. This approach not only reduces the required separation distance but also allows smoother control actions by replacing discrete braking commands with continuous deceleration trajectories. Recent studies on adaptive braking supervision show that incorporating real-time estimation of braking performance can significantly improve the utilisation of line capacity while maintaining certified safety margins (Goverde et al., 2013).

Communication latency introduces an additional dynamic constraint that directly affects the achievable minimum headway. In communication-based train control systems, the movement authority of the following train depends on the timely reception of position and speed information from the leading train and the control center. Even small delays in data transmission lead to an increase in the uncertainty of the predicted stopping point, which must be compensated by enlarging the safety buffer. Control-theoretic analyses show that this effect can be interpreted as a time-delay system in which stability and performance are strongly dependent on the update frequency of the communication channel. When latency exceeds a critical threshold, the control system must switch to more conservative operating modes, effectively reverting to quasi-static separation logic (Gong et al., 2023). Consequently, headway optimisation cannot be considered independently of communication performance, and joint design of control algorithms and data-exchange architectures becomes necessary.

Dwell time at stations represents another major control variable that influences headway dynamics at the network level. While running time regulation primarily affects train pairs in open track sections, dwell time variability propagates through the timetable and creates secondary conflicts. Traditional capacity models treat dwell time as an exogenous random variable; however, recent research demonstrates that it can be actively controlled through passenger-flow management, platform-door coordination, and adaptive departure strategies. Real-time dwell time control allows the system to absorb small delays locally and prevent their amplification along the line. Model predictive control frameworks integrating dwell time and speed regulation have been shown to increase line throughput by stabilising train sequences rather than by simply reducing minimum separation (Buchunde, 2024). This finding highlights that headway is not only a function of longitudinal motion but also of station operation dynamics.

The coupling effect between consecutive trains further reinforces the need for a system-level interpretation of headway. When separation decreases, the behaviour of one train becomes increasingly dependent on the control actions of its neighbours, forming a coupled dynamic system. In this regime, local control strategies based on pairwise spacing are no longer sufficient, because disturbances propagate through the entire train sequence. Cooperative control concepts, including virtual coupling and distributed optimisation, address this issue by synchronising acceleration and braking phases of multiple trains. Such approaches enable the formation of dynamically coordinated train platoons that operate with reduced separation while maintaining traffic stability. Recent experimental and simulation studies indicate that cooperative train control can significantly increase corridor capacity and reduce energy consumption through coordinated motion profiles (Quaglietta et al., 2022).

A critical implication of these developments is that headway can no longer be interpreted as a purely geometric or temporal measure. Instead, it emerges from the closed-loop interaction between control inputs, communication infrastructure, vehicle dynamics, and passenger-induced operational variability. Existing capacity assessment methodologies rarely capture this interaction, because they treat speed, braking, dwell time, and communication performance as independent parameters. Such decoupled representations fail to describe the feedback mechanisms that determine traffic stability and lead to overly optimistic or overly conservative estimates of achievable throughput (Schanzenbächer, 2020).

Furthermore, the simultaneous optimisation of these control parameters introduces multi-objective trade-offs that are absent in static models. For example, aggressive speed control can reduce headway but increase energy consumption and reduce passenger comfort, while longer dwell times may stabilise traffic at the cost of local capacity. Recent multi-objective optimisation studies demonstrate that optimal headway regulation requires balancing capacity, energy efficiency, and punctuality within a unified control framework (Ning et al., 2015). This confirms that headway dynamics should be analysed as part of an integrated performance optimisation problem rather than as an isolated safety constraint.

The interaction of the described control parameters forms a closed-loop structure in which headway is no longer a predefined constraint but an emergent dynamic variable determined by train motion control and real-time traffic conditions. This system-level interpretation is illustrated in [Figure 1](#F1).

FIGURE 1

![Flowchart illustrating the impact of dynamic control inputs—such as speed regulation, adaptive braking, dwell time control, train-to-train communication, and virtual coupling—on train motion dynamics, dynamic headway, traffic stability, and ultimately railway system capacity, emphasizing real-time monitoring and predictive optimization.](https://www.frontiersin.org/files/Articles/1826998/xml-images/ffutr-07-1826998-g001.webp)

Conceptual control framework of dynamic headway for railway capacity optimization.

The scheme illustrates the transformation of headway from a static safety constraint into a dynamically controlled system variable within a closed-loop control architecture. Real-time control inputs, including speed regulation, adaptive braking, dwell time management, communication performance, and cooperative train operation, directly influence train motion dynamics and trajectory evolution. The *Train Motion Dynamics* block represents the physical and operational behaviour of trains, including acceleration, braking processes, and interactions with infrastructure constraints. The resulting trajectory evolution determines the formation of time-space separation between consecutive trains, which defines the instantaneous headway. The *Traffic Stability & Flow Homogenization* block reflects the collective system response, including disturbance propagation, headway variance, and the emergence of stable or unstable traffic patterns. These factors directly affect system-level performance in terms of throughput, robustness, and energy-capacity interaction. The lower connection from *Train Motion Dynamics* to *Traffic Stability & Flow Homogenization* represents a feedback mechanism, in which traffic conditions influence subsequent control decisions. This feedback loop corresponds to predictive monitoring and continuous control adaptation, enabling real-time optimisation of headway and traffic flow. To ensure consistency, the terminology used in the figure (e.g., real-time control inputs) is aligned with the terminology used throughout the text.

In summary, dynamic headway is shaped by a set of interdependent control parameters that collectively determine the stability and throughput of railway traffic. Speed regulation provides the primary mechanism for real-time spacing control, adaptive braking transforms safety envelopes into continuously updated constraints, communication latency defines the feasible control horizon, dwell time management stabilises the temporal structure of operations, and cooperative train control introduces system-level coupling effects. The absence of integrated models capable of representing these interactions remains a major research gap and explains why many advanced signalling technologies have not yet achieved their full capacity potential in real operation.

## 4 Capacity as a system performance metric

The interpretation of railway capacity as a fixed property of infrastructure is increasingly being replaced by a dynamic, performance-oriented perspective in which the achievable traffic volume emerges from the interaction between operational variability, train dynamics, and control responsiveness. In this system view, capacity cannot be reduced to the inverse of a minimum headway or to a compressed timetable diagram; instead, it represents the maximum sustainable output that can be maintained without triggering unstable delay growth. This distinction becomes particularly evident when theoretical capacity values are compared with realised traffic performance under real operating conditions.

Recent trajectory-based analyses using reconstructed operational data show that the effective occupation of infrastructure differs significantly from planned occupation due to train heterogeneity and stochastic operational variations. In a 2024 microscopic capacity assessment, the dominant factor affecting realised capacity was not infrastructure geometry but the sequencing of trains with different running characteristics, while the impact of day-to-day operational variability remained secondary but non-negligible. This result indicates that capacity losses are primarily generated by dynamic interactions between trains rather than by static block occupation alone (Lordieck et al., 2024).

The gap between theoretical and operational capacity is therefore not simply a matter of safety margins but a manifestation of system dynamics. Compression-based methods implicitly assume that train paths can be arranged in a perfectly periodic structure, yet empirical studies consistently demonstrate that even small perturbations disrupt this periodicity and require recovery time that is not captured by static formulations. In a discrete-event simulation of freight operations under semi-automatic blocking, the realistic capacity of a line was estimated at approximately 69 trains per day when random dispatching delays were included, a value that closely matched observed performance but was significantly lower than deterministic estimates (Shukamanov et al., 2025). The reduction was not caused by longer nominal headways but by the temporal dispersion introduced by stochastic delays, which reduced the number of feasible train paths within the same time window. This confirms that operational capacity is governed by the variability of headway rather than by its minimum value.

The relationship between throughput and stability further illustrates why capacity must be treated as a dynamic system output. Increasing traffic density by reducing headway increases nominal throughput, but beyond a critical utilisation level the system enters a regime in which delays propagate nonlinearly. Data-driven analyses of freight corridors based on Swedish infrastructure reports show that high utilisation does not necessarily correlate with higher delays in a linear manner; instead, the relationship becomes highly sensitive to local conditions, indicating that the system transitions between stable and unstable operating states (Armah, 2025). This finding challenges the traditional assumption that capacity utilisation alone is a sufficient indicator of performance and highlights the importance of stability as a complementary metric.

The mechanism behind this behaviour lies in the propagation of disturbances through interacting train sequences. Algorithmic models of delay evolution on double-track lines demonstrate that once a disruption occurs, its cumulative impact depends on the structure of train interactions, the dispatching policy, and the available recovery margins. Performance indicators such as disruption settling time, number of affected trains, and cumulative delay provide a more realistic measure of system capacity than static headway values because they quantify the system’s ability to absorb perturbations (Ma et al., 2024). From this perspective, capacity is reached not when the infrastructure is fully occupied but when the system loses the ability to dissipate delays within an acceptable time horizon.

This dynamic interpretation is supported by predictive real-time traffic management models. Recent real-time simulation frameworks show that the instantaneous capacity of a railway line varies over time as a function of current traffic conditions and control actions. Instead of a single maximum value, capacity becomes a time-dependent envelope determined by the current state of the system (Tan et al., 2025). This result implies that offline capacity calculations cannot capture the actual performance limits of digitally controlled railways, where speed commands, departure times, and routing decisions are continuously updated.

At the network level, the cascading nature of delays provides further evidence that capacity is a systemic property. Systemic-risk analyses based on interaction networks between trains reveal that a small number of services may have a disproportionately large impact on overall performance due to shared resources and conflict points. By quantifying the “systemic impact” of individual trains, it becomes possible to identify critical elements whose regulation yields a higher increase in effective capacity than infrastructure expansion (Daniotti et al., 2023). This result reinforces the conclusion that capacity is governed by the topology of interactions and by control strategy rather than by physical infrastructure alone.

The growing availability of large-scale operational datasets has enabled the direct measurement of capacity as a function of reliability. For example, an integrated dataset covering the entire Finnish railway network from 2018 to 2024 revealed seasonal delay rates exceeding 25% in winter conditions, demonstrating that environmental variability alone can shift the achievable capacity envelope of a network (Borin et al., 2026). Such findings are incompatible with static capacity indicators and highlight the need for performance metrics that account for time-dependent external influences.

From a formal standpoint, the difference between theoretical and effective capacity can be interpreted through the role of headway variance. In idealised conditions, capacity is proportional to the inverse of the mean headway. In real operation, however, the effective throughput is reduced by the dispersion of headways and by the recovery time required after disturbances. This relationship explains why two lines with identical minimum headway can exhibit substantially different realised capacity and why adaptive control that reduces headway variance may increase throughput without reducing nominal separation.

The persistence of static capacity indicators in the literature reflects a methodological separation between safety verification and performance optimisation. In traditional approaches, safety constraints define the minimum headway, and capacity is calculated within these fixed limits. In dynamically controlled systems, safety and performance are coupled: the achievable capacity depends on the accuracy of state estimation, communication latency, and the predictive horizon of control algorithms. As a result, capacity becomes a controllable performance variable rather than an infrastructure constant.

Thus, capacity should be understood as the maximum traffic volume that can be sustained over a sufficiently long operational time horizon, such that delay propagation remains bounded and system performance does not degrade under realistic disturbance conditions. The difference between theoretical and operational capacity arises from headway variability, disturbance propagation, and the stability of train sequences. Throughput and stability form a nonlinear trade-off, and the achievable performance is determined by the system’s dynamic response rather than by static spacing rules. Real-time monitoring, predictive dispatching, and data-driven analysis further demonstrate that capacity is a time-dependent property that emerges from the interaction between infrastructure, rolling stock, environment, and control strategy. This system-level interpretation provides the necessary foundation for integrating dynamic headway control with capacity optimisation in the subsequent sections.

## 5 Modeling paradigms for headway control and capacity assessment

### 5.1 Analytical and traffic flow models

Analytical modelling remains the most “compact” way to connect headway regulation to capacity, because it turns the operational problem into explicit constraints and performance relationships that can be inspected, differentiated, and stress-tested. The price of this tractability is that many analytical formulations encode capacity as a consequence of static separation logic (minimum headway or blocking constraints) rather than as an output of a closed-loop controller reacting to disturbances. This methodological choice matters: it often produces capacity conclusions that are internally consistent mathematically, yet optimistic when transferred to real operations where dwell variability, communication delays, and control saturation dominate.

A large share of analytical capacity work is built on the blocking time representation and timetable compression logic (e.g., UIC-style approaches), where capacity is expressed through occupation times and minimum separations ([Abril et al., 2008](#B1); Landex et al., 2008). A representative recent example is the analytical UIC-406 compression model combined with blocking-time stairways proposed for a Chinese high-speed corridor. Instead of prescribing a fixed headway, the authors derive headway from operational data and embed it in a linear programming compression model; the case study reports that headway values on China HSR are “mainly limited” to about 4.5–5 min under the prevailing control constraints, and crucially shows that replacing fixed, rule-of-thumb separations by data-refined headway estimates yields measurable capacity effects. In their reported scenario, the occupation time computed under train-control-system assumptions was 842.75 min, while the blocking-time/headway-theory approach produced 65.42 min less occupation time for the same service pattern, indicating nontrivial headroom that purely conservative headway rules can hide (Wang et al., 2020). At the same time, it also exposes a limitation: the model’s gain is demonstrated mainly via re-parameterization (better headway estimation) rather than via an explicit control law that guarantees stability under stochastic perturbations. In other words, the analytical layer improves the nominal plan, but it does not yet certify that the plan is dynamically sustainable.

Traffic-flow theory and fundamental-diagram (FD) approaches attempt to lift the analysis from local headway constraints to system-level regimes (free flow, saturation, congestion), which is exactly what a “capacity as performance” framing demands (Zheng et al., 2024). Weik (2022) provides a particularly relevant discussion of when macroscopic FDs can meaningfully describe railway corridors with fixed-blocks and how these diagrams reveal operational phases and risks. The analysis explicitly spans block lengths from 500 m to 3 km, covering classical fixed-block operations and more segmented infrastructures that partially resemble continuous control. The paper contrasts deterministic “peak efficiency” regimes with stochastic settings (variability in arrivals and dwell times) and shows how small irregularities shift the system away from the deterministic envelope, i.e., capacity becomes a distribution of achievable flows rather than a single number (Weik, 2022). This is a key analytical insight for headway control: in a macroscopic regime description, the question is not merely “what is the minimum headway?” but “under what density and variability does the system remain on the stable branch of the FD?” The drawback is that FD models typically treat control only indirectly: they identify regimes and thresholds but rarely specify implementable, constraint-aware controllers that keep the system in the desired regime when disturbances occur. Consequently, FD-based capacity claims can still inherit the classic weakness the reviewer called out (“capacity counted without real-time performance”), unless they are paired with a control-consistent disturbance model.

A particularly important development in analytical modelling is the explicit inclusion of train-passenger interaction into macroscopic railway performance representations. Seo et al. (2023) derive a tractable FD that links train-flow (train/h), train-density (train/km), and passenger-flow, and they do so by starting from microscopic operation principles (boarding and cruising) and aggregating upward. One analytically consequential element is that dwell time becomes headway-dependent: the number of waiting passengers scales with headway, which in turn extends boarding time. In the paper’s formulation, dwell time includes a queuing-based component proportional to passenger demand and headway, plus a buffer term for door operations–embedding a feedback mechanism that can produce amplification (“bunching”) under high demand (Seo et al., 2023). This model class matters for headway control because it formalizes a mechanism by which aggressively tightened headways can backfire when the system is demand-saturated, smaller headways can increase interference and reduce effective speed/flow through passenger-induced dwell extensions, pushing the system toward the congested regime even without external incidents. For capacity assessment, that means any analytical approach that assumes dwell times are exogenous (or bounded by static margins) risks systematically mis-estimating the achievable throughput in peak periods, especially in metro-like contexts where passenger congestion is a first-order driver.

The strongest analytical models are those that

make the control variable explicit (speed, dwell, dispatch headway),

provide closed-form sensitivity relations (how capacity changes with block length, dwell variability, braking assumptions), and

expose regime changes (stability loss, “capacity drop”-like behavior) (Gašparík et al., 2025; Bulková et al., 2022).

Yet the analytical paradigm often fails precisely on the dimensions that matter most for dynamic headway control: closed-loop implementability and robustness. In blocking-time and timetable-compression formulations, disturbances are frequently represented as buffers or conservative margins; the approach can tell us how close the schedule is to a nominal limit, but it struggles to predict how fast the system degrades once variability exceeds the buffer. FD-based approaches improve on that by expressing state-dependent performance, but they still require an operational mapping from real-time measurements (density, headway variance, dwell demand) to admissible control actions (speed commands, holding, skipping, dispatch regulation) (Yousefi et al., 2026). Train-passenger analytical models move further by capturing endogenous dwell growth, but their calibration and network generalization can be challenging, and many results remain line-specific unless validated across different rolling-stock and station designs.

In practical terms, the analytical and traffic-flow paradigm is best viewed as the front-end of a modelling stack for capacity optimization: it excels at

rapid screening of design choices (block segmentation ranges, nominal headway targets),

deriving interpretable levers (which parameter dominates capacity in which regime), and

providing “sanity bounds” for more complex models.

It is least reliable when used alone to justify real-time capacity gains from tighter headways, because it tends to under-represent the very mechanisms that determine whether a nominal headway can be sustained–communication latency, stochastic dwell growth, controller saturation, and delay propagation. This is precisely why the field is progressively shifting toward hybrid formulations where analytical structure (constraints, regime logic) is retained but embedded into simulation/optimization and then informed by data-driven estimation.

This review article (published in *Frontiers in Future Transportation*, May 2026) provides a system-level analysis of dynamic headway control and its impact on railway capacity within closed-loop operational environments. Authored by Zhanibek Shukamanov (M.Kh. Dulaty Taraz University, Kazakhstan) and Gulfariza Suleimenova (ALT M. Tynyshpayev University, Kazakhstan), it critically assesses how train separation—traditionally a static safety constraint—can be treated as a controllable variable for real-time capacity optimization.

**Key Findings & Arguments:**
- Conventional planning-oriented capacity assessment systematically overestimates achievable throughput because it neglects traffic stability, disturbance propagation, and feedback-based regulation.
- The evolution from fixed-block to moving-block systems, predictive traffic management, and virtual coupling represents a shift from infrastructure-limited to control-limited capacity.
- Dynamic headway models using real-time trajectory prediction can reduce inter-train distance by over 60% while maintaining safety, but real-world gains are moderated by stochastic effects like dwell-time variability, heterogeneous rolling stock, and communication latency.
- Neglecting stochastic variability can lead to capacity overestimations of up to 30%.
- Capacity should be understood as a dynamic, time-dependent system property—the maximum sustainable throughput where delay propagation remains bounded—rather than a fixed infrastructure constant.

**Modeling Paradigms Reviewed:**
1. **Analytical & Traffic Flow Models** (e.g., UIC-406 compression, fundamental diagrams): compact and interpretable but tend to underrepresent closed-loop control, communication latency, and stochastic disturbances.
2. **Simulation & Optimization Approaches**: better capture real-time dynamics but are often developed in isolation from control-oriented formulations.
3. **Artificial Intelligence Approaches**: emerging but insufficiently integrated into safety-critical control.

**Control Parameters:** Speed regulation, adaptive braking, dwell time management, communication latency, and cooperative (virtual coupling) strategies all interact within a closed-loop framework to determine headway dynamics and system stability.

**Research Gaps & Future Directions:** The review identifies a lack of integrated real-time models linking headway control, traffic stability, and infrastructure utilization. It calls for future intelligent railway operation based on digital twins, reinforcement learning, and distributed coordination to enable continuous capacity regulation under stochastic conditions.

**Conclusion:** A unified conceptual framework is proposed linking control architecture, headway dynamics, traffic stability, and effective capacity within a cyber-physical control loop. The paper argues that safety and performance must be managed simultaneously through predictive and feedback control, rather than treated as separate concerns.

") [Versions Notes](https://www.mdpi.com/2076-0825/11/8/237/notes) ## Abstract Rail transit plays a significant role in the operation of an efficient and effective urban public transportation system. Safety and capacity are some of the most crucial objectives in railway operations. The communication-based train control (CBTC) system is a continuous and automatic train control system that realizes constant and high-capacity train ground two-way communication. In this study, a dynamic headway model of the ‘softwall’ moving-block approach is proposed for CBTC to increase the track capacity and improve dispatching efficiency based on the train trajectory prediction. For this precise trajectory prediction task, we introduce a hybrid trajectory prediction model to combine Long Short-term memory (LSTM) and Kalman Filter (KF) to extract the train’s local data features and learn the long-term dependencies, respectively. Then we present a dynamic headway model to maximize the train headway and reduce the track distance. The leading trains’ information is used to construct the iterative learning control strategy, and the predicted trajectory is input into the algorithm of the headway model. We use a simulation model of the rail network in Chengdu to demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed approach. The results show the Mean Absolute Error (MAE) of the predicted trajectory retreated to 93.97 cm and reductions in operation headway of at least 64.33% under the dynamic headway model versus the traditional moving-block model. Keywords: [LSTM-KF model](https://www.mdpi.com/search?q=LSTM-KF+model); [relative moving block](https://www.mdpi.com/search?q=relative+moving+block); [dynamic headway](https://www.mdpi.com/search?q=dynamic+headway) ## 1. Introduction The urban railway has been developed in recent decades with outstanding achievements worldwide. However, the existing operating capacity has dramatically hindered the transportation efficiency and development of urban rail transit. The limited operating capacity has led to traffic congestion, especially during the peak hours of the metropolis. The increasing demand for railway transportation has brought tremendous pressure to the existing railway transportation system, which is expected to alleviate frequent traffic jams. Efficiency implies shorter travel times, higher track capacity, and reduced congestion delays. The two primary ways to improve the efficiency of railway transportation are to increase the speed and the operation density, while the train operation speed has encountered a bottleneck. The minimum track headway, the optimum distance that the next train can achieve while following the lead train, is considered one of the major factors restricting operational capability. Therefore, transportation efficiency can be improved by increasing the operation density under the condition of the original railway network, which is achieved by shortening the tracking interval of the train. The two-way communication technology with a more significant amount of information transmission and fast transmission speed enables the increase of CBTC from a fixed-block system to a moving-block system. As shown in [Figure 1](https://www.mdpi.com/2076-0825/11/8/237#fig_body_display_actuators-11-00237-f001), the CBTC is a “moving-block” signaling system, which is based on the “concrete wall” principle, and trains are allowed to be separated by an absolute-braking distance (where it is assumed that a massive rock falls in front of the leading train). However, as the trajectory prediction is only determined by the absolute position of the front train, in order to guarantee safety, the minimum train separation is decided by the absolute-braking distance, which limits the improvement of the traffic density. ![Image 10: Actuators 11 00237 g001](https://www.mdpi.com/actuators/actuators-11-00237/article_deploy/html/images/actuators-11-00237-g001-550.jpg)[](https://www.mdpi.com/2076-0825/11/8/237#fig_body_display_actuators-11-00237-f001) **Figure 1.** Concrete and soft wall of CBTC system. Active communications in the CBTC system cause frequent information exchange between the control center and trains, including train dynamics and characteristics. This detailed information can lead to more modest but safe progress, considering train operation, speed, deceleration capabilities, etc. Therefore, we introduce trajectory prediction into the soft wall mode, enabling the more advanced calculation that considers that the leading train is running instead of stationary in the hard wall mode[[1](https://www.mdpi.com/2076-0825/11/8/237#B1-actuators-11-00237)]. Most trajectory prediction research focuses on pedestrians, aircraft, automobiles, and other fields, but the train is a sizeable inertial body and cannot stop as quickly as it detects danger. Moreover, the CBTC system is designed to be unable to release once emergency braking is applied under safety considerations, and we should avoid these situations as much as possible. Hence, one crucial task of our approach is to predict the accurate and long-term trajectories of the train, which covers the emergency braking time window of the following train to achieve safe and robust driving. Another task is to design a dynamic headway system for CBTC based on the predicted trajectory. It uses the future information to calculate its optimal safe distance relative to the lead train. Since such a headway is constantly updated, it is considered a dynamic headway. The dynamic track approach should also consider possible communication disruptions due to inclement weather or other failures and return gracefully and safely to a more conservative track without putting any trains at risk[[2](https://www.mdpi.com/2076-0825/11/8/237#B2-actuators-11-00237)]. The distinct features of the proposed system are: (1) The trajectory prediction part can accurately predict the leading train’s trajectory over the following one’s emergency braking time. (2) A dynamic headway policy based on vehicle-to-vehicle and vehicle-to-center communications results in much smaller distances than existing ones based on fixed-block and moving-block policies. (3) A backup switching policy increases gracefully to the new situation without sacrificing security, such as lost communications. In summary, the main contributions of this work are as follows: 1. Aiming at the trajectory prediction problem for trains, a data-processing method and a hybrid prediction model which enable an accurate prediction even when the horizons are increased to 15 s is established for the first time. 2. We used the concept of trajectory prediction and moving block and developed a soft wall control system that substantially reduces the distance between trains 3. In contrast to the traditional moving block, our proposed dynamic headway system shows reductions in train headway of at least 64%. The remainder of this paper is structured as follows. [Section 2](https://www.mdpi.com/2076-0825/11/8/237#sec2-actuators-11-00237) summarizes the research of headway policy and trajectory prediction in deep learning and the dynamic headway compared with these headway policies. [Section 3](https://www.mdpi.com/2076-0825/11/8/237#sec3-actuators-11-00237) introduces our proposed dynamic headway policy. [Section 4](https://www.mdpi.com/2076-0825/11/8/237#sec4-actuators-11-00237) presents the impact of headway selection on track capacity. The demonstration experiment of the proposed method is based on the established Chengdu Urban Railway simulation track network, and the results and analysis are presented. Finally, [Section 5](https://www.mdpi.com/2076-0825/11/8/237#sec5-actuators-11-00237) includes the conclusions of this work. ## 2. Related Work Here, we first present an overview of the dynamic headway policy and optimization methods in [Section 2.1](https://www.mdpi.com/2076-0825/11/8/237#sec2dot1-actuators-11-00237). Much research has been developed on the dynamic headway optimization of rail transit. We present a review of the trajectory prediction model in [Section 2.2](https://www.mdpi.com/2076-0825/11/8/237#sec2dot2-actuators-11-00237). ### 2.1. Dynamic Headway Policy and Optimization Methods Train schedule optimization and operating frequency settings are the directions of most of the literature. Typically, a regular ride schedule can reduce the total passenger wait time if the passenger arrivals fit a specific probability distribution model such as a uniform or Poisson distribution[[3](https://www.mdpi.com/2076-0825/11/8/237#B3-actuators-11-00237)]. Khoshniyat and Peterson propose the idea of maintaining a minimum travel interval concerning travel time, in which the arrival time of the train is not a fixed size period but leaves a triangular period[[4](https://www.mdpi.com/2076-0825/11/8/237#B4-actuators-11-00237)]. A real-time headway control system for maintaining headway regularity in railway networks is presented by Xun et al.[[5](https://www.mdpi.com/2076-0825/11/8/237#B5-actuators-11-00237)]. Xin yang et al.[[6](https://www.mdpi.com/2076-0825/11/8/237#B6-actuators-11-00237)] proposed a train scheduling optimization method to reduce energy consumption and running time. The test on the Beijing subway line shows that their method can reduce travel time by 3.26%. When the design of the controller can directly lead to the change of train headway, the introduction of controlled optimization is practical. Therefore, the controller design has always been a research hotspot in the train operation control system under moving-block mode. Li et al.[[7](https://www.mdpi.com/2076-0825/11/8/237#B7-actuators-11-00237)] adopted a linear quadratic regular with Gaussian distribution to design a state feedback control method for metro. Sanchez-Martinez et al.[[8](https://www.mdpi.com/2076-0825/11/8/237#B8-actuators-11-00237)] proposed a mathematical model for holding control optimization to regulate the train following headway, which takes the dynamic running time of trains into account. Some researchers put forward the viewpoint of cooperative train control. Dong et al.[[9](https://www.mdpi.com/2076-0825/11/8/237#B9-actuators-11-00237)] present cooperative control methods and corresponding stability criteria for multiple trains under moving-block signaling systems and proposed corresponding control algorithms established using Lyapunov and invariant-set theorems. References[[10](https://www.mdpi.com/2076-0825/11/8/237#B10-actuators-11-00237),[11](https://www.mdpi.com/2076-0825/11/8/237#B11-actuators-11-00237),[12](https://www.mdpi.com/2076-0825/11/8/237#B12-actuators-11-00237)] introduced the multi-agent system control theory into train-coordinated operation. An adaptive coordinated control algorithm based on the LaSalles invariance principle is adopted in[[10](https://www.mdpi.com/2076-0825/11/8/237#B10-actuators-11-00237)] to keep the headway distances of each train with its neighboring trains stabilized at safe stationary distances. Given the limited effect of most headway optimization based on the existing moving-block mode, recent research usually focuses on the control policy of headway. In reference[[2](https://www.mdpi.com/2076-0825/11/8/237#B2-actuators-11-00237)], a dynamic headway regulation framework for a positive train control (PTC) system was proposed to improve track capacity and safety in railway operation by integrating a dynamic dispatching model. H Ye et al.[[13](https://www.mdpi.com/2076-0825/11/8/237#B13-actuators-11-00237),[14](https://www.mdpi.com/2076-0825/11/8/237#B14-actuators-11-00237)] reported optimal train speed controls of multiple trains under both fixed-block and moving-block systems. F shi et al.[[15](https://www.mdpi.com/2076-0825/11/8/237#B15-actuators-11-00237)] present a model to minimize the number of train trips and design a heuristic algorithm to maximize the train headway. Consequently, improved studies considering flexible headways were proposed in[[16](https://www.mdpi.com/2076-0825/11/8/237#B16-actuators-11-00237),[17](https://www.mdpi.com/2076-0825/11/8/237#B17-actuators-11-00237)]. Sangphong and Ratanavaraha proposed a method to determine the minimum train headway through the train speed and the maximum block length in the fixed-block system to improve the line capacity as much as possible[[18](https://www.mdpi.com/2076-0825/11/8/237#B18-actuators-11-00237)]. Research[[19](https://www.mdpi.com/2076-0825/11/8/237#B19-actuators-11-00237)] shows a study on the optimization of the train headway in the planning phase under the planned transportation mode. Xiang Li et al.[[20](https://www.mdpi.com/2076-0825/11/8/237#B20-actuators-11-00237)] developed a headway optimization model based on the proposed concept of measuring the uniformity of headway distribution. It is worth mentioning that the current information of adjacent vehicles is used for processing, which is received by the rear train after the communication delay in most of the literature mentioned above. The optimization effect of headway can be significantly improved considering more information containing future status and characteristics of trains. Therefore, we introduce a hybrid trajectory prediction model into our dynamic headway policy. ### 2.2. Trajectory Prediction As an effective tool for mining large amounts of data, neural networks have been widely used in data-driven trajectory prediction. With advances in artificial intelligence, various Deep Neural Networks (DNN) have been implemented on trajectory prediction. Among these, Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) have been designed to deal with time sequence data based on the recurrent architecture in the network. Because of the dynamic nature of the traffic system, RNN is particularly well-suited to capture the temporal and spatial evolution of traffic flow, capacity, and speed, and has certain advantages when learning the nonlinear properties of time sequences. Kong et al.[[21](https://www.mdpi.com/2076-0825/11/8/237#B21-actuators-11-00237)] present an innovative approach by utilizing the deep-stacking network method for hazardous risk based on multisource data monitored by the Internet of Things. Liu et al.[[22](https://www.mdpi.com/2076-0825/11/8/237#B22-actuators-11-00237)] proposed the spatial temporal-RNN (ST-RNN) algorithm, which uses the historical spatiotemporal data of moving objects to train the RNN network to predict the location of the user at a certain point in time. Al-Molegi et al.[[23](https://www.mdpi.com/2076-0825/11/8/237#B23-actuators-11-00237)] improved the algorithm, and their proposed Space Time Features-based-RNN (STF-RNN) algorithm achieved better prediction accuracy. Research[[24](https://www.mdpi.com/2076-0825/11/8/237#B24-actuators-11-00237),[25](https://www.mdpi.com/2076-0825/11/8/237#B25-actuators-11-00237)] used an LSTM-based structure with time serial states of the target vehicle and ego vehicle. Berenguer et al.[[26](https://www.mdpi.com/2076-0825/11/8/237#B26-actuators-11-00237)] extend the Social-LSTM model with a context-pooling layer. Li Z et al.[[27](https://www.mdpi.com/2076-0825/11/8/237#B27-actuators-11-00237)] developed a long short-term memory network to build the train dynamic model in a nonparametric way. The Soial GAN model was proposed in[[28](https://www.mdpi.com/2076-0825/11/8/237#B28-actuators-11-00237)] by combining tools from sequence prediction and generative adversarial networks: a recurrent sequence-to-sequence model observes motion histories and predicts future behavior. Jin et al.[[29](https://www.mdpi.com/2076-0825/11/8/237#B29-actuators-11-00237)] propose a novel planar flow-based variational auto-encoder prediction model (PFVAE), which uses the LSTM as the auto-encoder and designs the variational auto-encoder (VAE) as a time series data predictor to overcome the noise effects. Chen et al.[[30](https://www.mdpi.com/2076-0825/11/8/237#B30-actuators-11-00237)] propose a stacked Bidirectional Gated Recurrent Unit neural network model to predict the traffic speed of the expressway over different estimation time intervals. Zhao, T.et al.[[31](https://www.mdpi.com/2076-0825/11/8/237#B31-actuators-11-00237)] model the interactions and constraints jointly within a Multi-Agent Tensor Fusion (MATF) network that from the scene context and the stochasticity network decodes recurrently to multiple agents’ future trajectories. Deo, N.et al.[[32](https://www.mdpi.com/2076-0825/11/8/237#B32-actuators-11-00237)] proposed an LSTM encoder–decoder model that uses convolutional social pooling as an improvement to social pooling layers for robustly learning interdependencies in vehicle motion. ## 3. Train Dynamic Headway Policy In this section, the dynamic headway policy architecture is proposed. The framework comprises three parts, as shown in [Figure 2](https://www.mdpi.com/2076-0825/11/8/237#fig_body_display_actuators-11-00237-f002), which are the trajectory prediction, headway calculation, and headway policy switch. The details of the system architecture and functions are described as follows. ![Image 11: Actuators 11 00237 g002](https://www.mdpi.com/actuators/actuators-11-00237/article_deploy/html/images/actuators-11-00237-g002-550.jpg)[](https://www.mdpi.com/2076-0825/11/8/237#fig_body_display_actuators-11-00237-f002) **Figure 2.** Headway control loop. ### 3.1. Trajectory Prediction of Leading Train Traditional deep-learning algorithms, such as RNN, are calculated sequentially, which means the relevant algorithms can only be calculated according to the order of the internal structure of the model. In such algorithms, the results of time t depend on the value of the previous time, which limits the parallel ability of the model with the information loss in the calculation process. We propose a hybrid LSTM model with a KF filter based on our previous work[[33](https://www.mdpi.com/2076-0825/11/8/237#B33-actuators-11-00237)]. LSTM is a particular RNN network used to solve the problems of gradient disappearance and gradient explosion in long sequence training. At the same time, the Kalman Filter (KF) is a prediction method based on linear regression, which is commonly used in the field of mobile robots. Our main idea is to integrate both advantages of KF and LSTM in exploring the train’s trajectory prediction, in which the KF model is used to extract the train’s local data features, whereas the LSTM model is applied to process time-series data and learn the long-term dependencies of train trajectory data. The structure of the trajectory predictor is shown in [Figure 3](https://www.mdpi.com/2076-0825/11/8/237#fig_body_display_actuators-11-00237-f003). ![Image 12: Actuators 11 00237 g003](https://www.mdpi.com/actuators/actuators-11-00237/article_deploy/html/images/actuators-11-00237-g003-550.jpg)[](https://www.mdpi.com/2076-0825/11/8/237#fig_body_display_actuators-11-00237-f003) **Figure 3.** The process of trajectory prediction. In the LSTM structure, the input gate control updates and stores information, the forget gate control deletes information, and the output gate controls the final unit output. $$ f_{t} = \sigma \left(\right. W_{f} \cdot \left[\right. h_{t - 1} , x_{t} \left]\right. + b_{f} \left.\right) $$ (1) $$ i_{t} = \sigma \left(W_{i}\cdot\left[h_{t - 1},x_{t}\right]+b_{i}\right) $$ (2) $$ o_{t} = \sigma \left(W_{o}\left[h_{t - 1},x_{t}\right]+b_{o}\right) $$ (3) The value $\left(\overset{\sim}{C}\right)_{t}$ is the candidate cell state which can be represented as: $$ \left(\overset{\sim}{C}\right)_{t} = tanh \left(W_{C}\cdot\left[h_{t - 1},x_{t}\right]+b_{C}\right) $$ (4) $C_{t}$ is the new state combined with the previous $C_{t - 1}$ and the candidate states $\left(\overset{\sim}{C}\right)_{t}$. $$ C_{t} = f_{t} * C_{t - 1} + i_{t} * \left(\overset{\sim}{C}\right)_{t} $$ (5) Finally, the output gate decides the final output from the cell state: $$ h_{t} = o_{t} * tanh \left(C_{t}\right) $$ (6) where ∗ denotes the Hadamard product, and$\sigma$ denotes the standard logistics sigmoid function, $f_{t}$, $i_{t}$, $o_{t}$ are the output of different gates, $C_{t}$ is the new state of memory cell, $\left(\overset{\sim}{C}\right)_{t}$ is the final state of the memory cell and $h_{t}$ is the final output of the memory unit. $W_{f} , W_{i} , W_{c} , W_{o}$ denote the weight matrices in each layer. Kalman filtering is a linear optimal filtering algorithm suitable for linear Gaussian systems and does not need to save past measurement data. It uses the current, previous data, and system state equation estimation to correct and predict the new state estimation value. It is assumed that the state of the train’s navigation track at time t is: We use the state variable matrix $x_{k} \left(\right. t \left.\right)$ to represent the state of the train k at time t. args.summary:
This is a peer-reviewed scientific article titled "Communication-Based Train Control with Dynamic Headway Based on Trajectory Prediction," published in the journal *Actuators* (MDPI, 2022, Volume 11, Issue 8, Article 237). The authors are Yijuan He, Jidong Lv, and Tao Tang, affiliated with Beijing Jiaotong University, China.

The study proposes a dynamic headway model for Communication-Based Train Control (CBTC) systems using a "soft wall" moving-block approach to increase track capacity and improve dispatching efficiency. The key innovation is the use of a hybrid trajectory prediction model combining Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks and Kalman Filter (KF) to predict the leading train's trajectory and enable closer, safer train following.

**Methodology:**
- A hybrid LSTM-KF model predicts the leading train's trajectory over the following train's emergency braking time window (15 seconds).
- A dynamic headway model uses predicted trajectories to calculate optimal safe distances between trains.
- A backup switching policy degrades to conservative moving-block mode in case of communication failure.

**Key Results:**
- The Mean Absolute Error (MAE) of the predicted trajectory was reduced to 93.97 cm.
- Reductions in operation headway of at least 64.33% under the dynamic headway model versus the traditional moving-block model.
- The experiment used a simulation model of the rail network in Chengdu, China.

**Main Contributions:**
1. A data-processing method and hybrid prediction model enabling accurate trajectory prediction even when horizons are extended to 15 seconds.
2. A soft wall control system that substantially reduces the distance between trains using trajectory prediction and moving-block concepts.
3. Demonstration of at least 64% reduction in train headway compared to traditional moving-block systems.

*Creating Smart Rail Services Using Digital Technologies*

# Dynamic Headway and Its Role in Future Railways

**Making the Transition from Scheduled to Demand-Response Services**

## Highlight

Dynamic Headway is the world’s first solution that offers new rail transport value in the form of flexible rail services based on passenger demand. It analyzes demand conditions with data acquired from sensors installed in stations and trains, and automatically optimizes the number of train services in response to the analyzed demand. It provides value to passengers in the form of congestion alleviation and transport comfort, and to rail service operators in the form of improved service efficiency. Hitachi is currently working on a proof of concept for the solution with Italian railway systems integrator, Ansaldo STS, and Denmark’s Copenhagen Metro. As part of these activities, Hitachi has assessed the customer value that Dynamic Headway will bring by using simulations to evaluate its quantitative and qualitative benefits. Hitachi will continue to develop and release solutions driven by digital technologies as it aims to help achieve a more comfortable society to live in through rail transport.
